title: Soergel Intersection Forms and Hodge Theory

items.title: The real type-A Soergel category by scalar extension
items.statement:
**Scalar extension of the published realization.** The published type-A page
works over $k=\mathbb Q$ with the polynomial ring $R=\mathbb Q[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$
and the two normalizations of the simple roots of
[[def-type-a-reflection-realization-and-polynomial-ring]]: the coordinate roots
$\beta_i=x_i-x_{i+1}$ and the alternating balanced roots
$\alpha_i^{\mathrm{bal}}=\varepsilon_i\beta_i$, $\varepsilon_i=(-1)^{i-1}$. For
the Hodge-theoretic statements of this page we extend scalars along
$\mathbb Q\hookrightarrow\mathbb R$ and set
$$S:=\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n],\qquad \deg x_i=2,$$
with $S_0=\mathbb R$ and finite-dimensional homogeneous pieces $S_d$; the
symmetric group $S_n$ acts by the place permutations
$w\cdot x_i:=x_{w(i)}$ ([[def-type-a-reflection-realization-and-polynomial-ring]]).
On this page $\alpha_i$ always means the coordinate root
$\alpha_i:=\beta_i=x_i-x_{i+1}$, and $\alpha_i^\vee:=\beta_i^\vee$ is the
coordinate coroot, so that under the standard form the Cartan entries are
$\langle\alpha_i^\vee,\alpha_j\rangle=2\delta_{ij}-\delta_{|i-j|,1}$ and
adjacent entries are $-1$; the reflection is
$s_i(v)=v-\langle v,\alpha_i\rangle\alpha_i^\vee$. The alternating balanced
roots $\alpha_i^{\mathrm{bal}}$ are retained by the published page for its
diagrammatic presentation and are not used for positivity, Demazure traces or
descent signs on this page; both choices define the same reflections, the same
reflecting hyperplanes, the same invariant rings $S^{s_i}$ and the same
underlying bimodules, and they differ only by the unit $\pm1$ in front of the
root, which changes no tensor bimodule but does change the normalization of
$\partial_i$ and of the trace.

**The real generators and the real category.** For $1\le i\le n-1$ set
$$B_i^R:=S\otimes_{S^{s_i}}S(1),$$
the balanced tensor product of the $(S,S^{s_i})$-bimodule $S$ with the
$(S^{s_i},S)$-bimodule $S$, shifted in the Elias-Williamson convention
$M(1)_d=M_{d+1}$ used on this page ([[def-type-a-soergel-bimodule-for-a-simple-reflection]],
[[def-graded-ring-module-bimodule-and-internal-shift]]). Its left basis
$\{1\otimes1,\,1\otimes\alpha_i\}$ and right basis
$\{1\otimes1,\,\alpha_i\otimes1\}$ have degrees $-1$ and $+1$, and
$B_i^R$ is finite free of rank two on each side
([[lem-type-a-soergel-generators-are-finite-free-on-both-sides]]). The **real
type-A Soergel category** $\mathrm{SBim}_n^R$ is the idempotent completion
([[def-the-type-a-soergel-category]]) of the full subcategory of graded
$(S,S)$-bimodules whose objects are the finite direct sums of shifts
$B_{\underline i}^R(d)=B_{i_1}^R\otimes_S\cdots\otimes_SB_{i_r}^R(d)$ of real
Bott-Samelson products ([[def-bott-samelson-bimodule-of-a-word]]), with the
same internal shifts as the rational category, i.e. $M(d)_e=M_{d+e}$ in the
Elias-Williamson convention. Its unit is the graded ring $S$ itself, regarded
as an object in cohomological degree zero; it is not a polynomial ring
concentrated in internal degree zero. Categorically,
$\mathrm{SBim}_n^R=\mathrm{Kar}(\mathrm{BSBim}_n^R)$ has the same formal
properties as the rational Soergel category: it is graded, additive,
idempotent-complete and monoidal with unit $S$, and every object is a finite
direct sum of graded shifts of indecomposables.

**Scalar extension of objects.** For a graded $(R,R)$-bimodule $M$ over the
rational polynomial ring put $M^R:=M\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb R$, with the
$S$-actions induced from the $R$-actions and the tensor grading. Since
$\mathbb Q\to\mathbb R$ is flat, scalar extension is exact on graded pieces;
it carries the rational generator $B_i=R\otimes_{R^{s_i}}R(1)$ to $B_i^R$, the
rational Bott-Samelson construction to the real one, and the rational
idempotent completion to the real one. Standard graph supports, the
$\Delta$- and $\nabla$-flags with their characters, and all formulas of the
rational page are read over $\mathbb R$ after extension. The Hecke algebra
used for characters is the integral normalized algebra
$H_v(n)$ over $\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ with basis $H_x$ of
[[def-split-grothendieck-rings-of-type-a-soergel-categories]]; it is the same
algebra before and after the scalar extension, since it is defined over
$\mathbb Z$.

**The dominant chamber.** The **dominant chamber** on this page is the set of
strictly dominant degree-two elements
$$\Theta:=\Bigl\{\rho=\sum_{j=1}^n c_jx_j\ :\ c_j\in\mathbb R,\ c_j>c_{j+1}\ \text{for } 1\le j\le n-1\Bigr\}\subset S_2 .$$
It is nonempty, for example for $c_j=(n+1)/2-j$, which gives
$c_j-c_{j+1}=1$ for every $j$. For $\rho=\sum_jc_jx_j$ the coordinate
evaluation is $\rho(\alpha_i^\vee)=\rho(x_i-x_{i+1})=c_i-c_{i+1}$, so
$\rho\in\Theta$ is exactly a degree-two element with
$\rho(\alpha_i^\vee)>0$ for every simple coroot; no alternating-sign chamber
and no replacement of $\rho$ is used anywhere on this page.

**Conventions.** All tensor products are over $S$ unless indicated, all shifts
are the internal shifts just fixed, "form" on this page always means a graded
symmetric form that is $S$-bilinear for the right action and invariant under
the left action in the sense fixed by the intersection-form definition below, and
dimensions of reduced modules are always real dimensions. The rational
comparison statements needed for labels, characters and forms are collected
in the comparison lemma later on this page.
items.strategy: The place permutation action and coordinate roots/coroots are explicitly supplied by the published two-normalization realization. We fix the coordinate choice for every alpha, Demazure trace and positivity condition on this Hodge page. The invariant-ring tensor bimodules do not change when a root is multiplied by -1; only the chosen Demazure/trace normalization changes, so no diagrammatic presentation is silently reinterpreted. The polynomial ring has S_0=R and finite-dimensional homogeneous pieces. Flat extension of Q to R commutes with the finite free presentations, invariant decomposition S=S^{s_i}⊕alpha_i S^{s_i}, shifts and tensor products. The idempotent closure is the defined real category; preservation of rational indecomposable labels is proved separately in the comparison lemma. For rho=Σ c_jx_j, rho(alpha_i^vee)=c_i-c_{i+1}; the displayed decreasing coefficients give value 1 at every simple coroot. These are the positive roots x_a-x_b for a<b used by inversion length, with adjacent Cartan entries -1. No alternating-sign dominant chamber or unverified replacement of rho is used.

items.title: The Hecke trace form, its values on the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis, and the standard pairing
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** induction on the length in the standard basis; the ambient algebra is finite free over $A$.

1.1 **Well-definedness and bilinearity (1), (2).** Since $\{H_w\}$ is an $A$-basis by [F1], prescribing $\varepsilon(H_w)=\delta_{e,w}$ and extending $A$-linearly is well defined and unique; the reversal map $a$ is a well-defined $A$-linear anti-automorphism by [F2], and multiplication is $A$-bilinear, so $(h,h')=\varepsilon(a(h)h')$ is a well-defined $A$-bilinear form, for $(ph,qh')=\varepsilon(p\,a(h)\,q\,h')=pq\,\varepsilon(a(h)h')$ with $p,q\in A$. This proves (1) and (2). [given, F1, F2]

2.1 **The key identity: base case and recursion.** We prove by induction on $\ell(u)$ that $\varepsilon(H_uH_y)=\delta_{u,y^{-1}}$ for all $u,y\in S_n$; for $u=e$ this reads $H_eH_y=H_y$ and $\varepsilon(H_y)=\delta_{e,y}=\delta_{u,y^{-1}}$, and for $u\ne e$ we choose a simple reflection $s$ with $\ell(us)=\ell(u)-1$ and note that [F1] applied to $w=us$ gives $H_{us}H_s=H_u$, since $(us)s=u$ has length $\ell(u)=\ell(us)+1$. [base, step 1.1, F1, F2]

3.1 **The left multiplication rule.** Applying the anti-automorphism $a$ of [F2] to the two cases of [F1] and using $a(H_wH_s)=a(H_s)a(H_w)=H_sH_{w^{-1}}$ and $(ws)^{-1}=sw^{-1}$ gives $H_sH_w=H_{sw}$ if $\ell(sw)=\ell(w)+1$, and $H_sH_w=H_{sw}+(v^{-1}-v)H_w$ if $\ell(sw)<\ell(w)$; this is the rule used in the two cases below. [step 2.1, F1, F2]

4.1 **The ascent case.** Keep $u\ne e$ and its right descent $s$ from step 2.1, and let $y\in S_n$ satisfy $\ell(sy)>\ell(y)$. Then $H_sH_y=H_{sy}$ by step 3.1, so $\varepsilon(H_uH_y)=\varepsilon(H_{us}H_sH_y)=\varepsilon(H_{us}H_{sy})$; the induction hypothesis applies to the pair $(us,sy)$, whose first length is $\ell(u)-1$, giving $\varepsilon(H_{us}H_{sy})=\delta_{us,(sy)^{-1}}=\delta_{us,y^{-1}s}$, and $us=y^{-1}s$ holds if and only if $u=y^{-1}$ (multiply on the right by $s$ and use $s^2=e$), so $\varepsilon(H_uH_y)=\delta_{u,y^{-1}}$. [step 3.1, ih]

5.1 **The descent case.** Keep $u,s$ as above and let $\ell(sy)<\ell(y)$. Then $H_sH_y=H_{sy}+(v^{-1}-v)H_y$ by step 3.1, so $\varepsilon(H_uH_y)=\varepsilon(H_{us}H_{sy})+(v^{-1}-v)\varepsilon(H_{us}H_y)$; the induction hypothesis gives $\varepsilon(H_{us}H_{sy})=\delta_{us,y^{-1}s}$ and $\varepsilon(H_{us}H_y)=\delta_{us,y^{-1}}$. If $us=y^{-1}$, then $y=(us)^{-1}=su^{-1}$ and, since $us$ is a right descent of $u$, taking inverses gives $\ell(y)=\ell(su^{-1})=\ell(us)=\ell(u)-1$, while $\ell(sy)=\ell(u^{-1})=\ell(u)>\ell(y)$, contradicting $\ell(sy)<\ell(y)$; hence $\delta_{us,y^{-1}}=0$ and $\varepsilon(H_uH_y)=\delta_{us,y^{-1}s}=\delta_{u,y^{-1}}$. [step 4.1, ih]

6.1 **The induction concludes.** For every $u\ne e$ the cases $\ell(sy)>\ell(y)$ and $\ell(sy)<\ell(y)$ exhaust all $y$ for the chosen right descent $s$, and each case reduced the first argument's length; with the base case this proves $\varepsilon(H_uH_y)=\delta_{u,y^{-1}}$ for all $u,y\in S_n$. [step 2.1, step 4.1, step 5.1]

7.1 **Standard orthonormality (4).** For all $x,y$, using $a(H_x)=H_{x^{-1}}$ from [F2] and step 6.1 with $u=x^{-1}$, we get $(H_x,H_y)=\varepsilon(a(H_x)H_y)=\varepsilon(H_{x^{-1}}H_y)=\delta_{x^{-1},y^{-1}}=\delta_{x,y}$, the last equality being injectivity of $w\mapsto w^{-1}$; this proves (4). [step 6.1, F2]

7.2 **The generator trace identity.** By step 6.1, for every $w$ and simple reflection $s$ one has $\varepsilon(H_wH_s)=\delta_{w,s^{-1}}=\delta_{w,s}$ and $\varepsilon(H_sH_w)=\delta_{s,w^{-1}}=\delta_{w,s}$. Extending over the standard basis gives $\varepsilon(zH_s)=\varepsilon(H_sz)$ for every $z\in H$. In particular the common value for $w=s$ is $1$. [step 6.1, F1, algebra]

8.1 **$\varepsilon$ is a trace and yields the adjunctions (3).** Every element of $H$ is a finite $A$-linear combination of words in the generators, and moving each letter of a word for the second factor to the front one at a time with step 7.2 and bilinearity shows $\varepsilon(xy)=\varepsilon(yx)$ for all $x,y\in H$; consequently, for simple $s$ and $h,h'\in H$, using $a(H_s)=H_s$ from [F2], $(hH_s,h')=\varepsilon(a(hH_s)h')=\varepsilon(H_sa(h)h')=\varepsilon(a(h)h'H_s)=(h,h'H_s)$ and $(H_sh,h')=\varepsilon(a(h)a(H_s)h')=\varepsilon(a(h)H_sh')=(h,H_sh')$, which proves (3) and shows both left and right multiplication by $H_s$ are self-adjoint for $(-,-)$. [step 7.2, F2, algebra]

8.2 **Values on the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis (5).** Write $\underline H_x=\sum_{u\le x}h_{u,x}H_u$ with $h_{u,x}=p_{u,x}\in\mathbb Z[v]$, $h_{x,x}=1$ and $h_{u,x}\in v\mathbb Z[v]$ for $u<x$, all other coefficients zero, as in [F3]; then bilinearity (2) and orthonormality from step 7.1 give $(\underline H_x,\underline H_y)=\sum_uh_{u,x}h_{u,y}$. A nonzero term requires $u\le x$ and $u\le y$; if $x\ne y$, every surviving term has a factor in $v\mathbb Z[v]$, because $u<x$ or $u<y$ is [F3], and $u=x\ne y$ gives $h_{x,y}\in v\mathbb Z[v]$ when $x<y$ and $h_{x,y}=0$ otherwise, symmetrically for $u=y$; hence $(\underline H_x,\underline H_y)\in v\mathbb Z[v]$ for $x\ne y$. For $x=y$ the term $u=x$ contributes $h_{x,x}^2=1$ and every other term has $u<x$ and contributes to $v^2\mathbb Z[v]$, so $(\underline H_x,\underline H_x)\in 1+v\mathbb Z[v]$. [step 7.1, F3, algebra]

9.1 **The standard pairing (6) and conclusion.** By (4) the form $(-,-)$ is the $A$-bilinear form whose matrix in the normalized standard basis $\{H_x\}$ is the identity; the published type-A Soergel Hom formula uses the standard pairing with $\langle H_x,H_y\rangle=\delta_{xy}$ on that normalized basis, and the dictionary of [F4] fixes the normalization $H_x=v^{\ell(x)}T_x$ and the resulting Kazhdan-Lusztig coefficients, so the transported pairing agrees with $(-,-)$ on the basis and hence on $H$ by bilinearity. All six clauses are proved over $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$, using only existence and triangularity of the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis and no positivity and no choice. [step 8.1, step 8.2, F3, F4, discharge-induction: step 5.1] ∎

items.title: Indecomposable type-A Soergel bimodules are classified by their normalized top support
items.statement: Over $k=\mathbb Q$ or $k=\mathbb R$, the bimodule Soergel category has unique finite Krull-Schmidt decompositions. For every $x\in S_n$ there is a unique normalized indecomposable $B_x$ supported on $\{y:y\le x\}$ with top $\Delta$ layer exactly $\Delta_x=R_x(-\ell(x))$. It is the unique summand with the $x$ graph of any reduced Bott-Samelson word for $x$. Every indecomposable is exactly one $B_x(d)$. Its finite-dimensional degree-zero endomorphism algebra is local, with residue field $k$ under restriction to its rank-one top layer. No Kazhdan-Lusztig character identity is assumed.
items.strategy:
1.1 A finite-dimensional endomorphism algebra and the absence of nontrivial idempotents imply locality. Indeed for an endomorphism $f$ its polynomial minimal relation splits into a power of $T$ and a factor coprime to $T$. The polynomial Chinese remainder identity produces an idempotent separating the nilpotent and invertible parts; indecomposability forces one part to vanish. Thus every $f$ is invertible or nilpotent, and a nonunit $f$ has $1-f$ invertible. Nonunits form a two-sided ideal: multiplication cannot make a nonunit invertible in a finite-dimensional algebra; if two nonunits summed to a unit, dividing their sum would express $1$ as two nonunits, contradicting the invertibility of $1-f$. This is the unique maximal ideal. Its powers eventually vanish: if a power stabilizes, take a minimal finite generating list for that stable ideal and express its last generator using coefficients in the maximal ideal; the invertibility of $1-a$ for such a coefficient eliminates that generator, a contradiction. [F1, algebra]

2.1 Split idempotents until indecomposable summands remain. Each split reduces the positive right rank of its summand, so there are only finitely many splits. The resulting summands have local endomorphism rings by step 1.1. Decompositions are unique: in two finite decompositions, express the identity of one indecomposable as the sum of its composites through the summands of the other. The local maximal ideal cannot contain every composite; an invertible composite gives a split inclusion into one indecomposable summand, hence an isomorphism to it. Remove the common summand and repeat. This proves finite Krull-Schmidt existence and uniqueness. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Decompose a reduced word for $x$. Its top layer is a single $\Delta_x$ by [F4], and the top-layer functor is additive by [F2]. Exactly one indecomposable summand therefore has this graph, with precisely this normalized layer; call it $B_x$. All other summands have support strictly below $x$. This constructs a normalized candidate without any character conjecture. [F2, F4, step 2.1]

4.1 Let $M$ be any nonzero Soergel object and choose a maximal support label $x$. The two graph layers $\Gamma_xM$ and $\Gamma^xM$ are identified by multiplication by $p_x$ as in [F2]. Choose one homogeneous basis element $m$ of the latter, and let $d$ make its degree equal to the generator degree of $\Gamma^xB_x(d)$. Choose graph maps $f_0:\Gamma^xB_x(d)\to\Gamma^xM$ taking that generator to $m$, and $g_0:\Gamma_xM\to\Gamma_xB_x(d)$ which takes the corresponding element $p_xm$ to the generator $p_xb$ and kills the other basis elements. These maps are homogeneous of degree zero and satisfy the identity on the rank-one $x$ layer. [F2, step 3.1, choose]

5.1 Lift these maps to bimodule maps $f:B_x(d)\to M$ and $g:M\to B_x(d)$. The quotient map $M\to\Gamma^xM$ is the last step of a $\nabla$ flag with $x$ last; its kernel is flagged, so [F3] lifts the map $B_x(d)\to\Gamma^xM$. The inclusion $\Gamma_xM\to M$ is the first step of a $\Delta$ flag with $x$ first; its quotient is flagged, so [F3] lifts $g_0$ followed by $\Gamma_xB_x(d)\to B_x(d)$. The first lifted map on the quotient and the second on the submodule agree with the prescribed graph maps. The image identity $\Gamma_xM=\Gamma^xM p_x$ makes their composite $gf$ act as the identity on $\Gamma_xB_x(d)$. Thus $gf$ is not nilpotent, and is invertible by step 1.1. Rescale $g$ by its inverse to exhibit $B_x(d)$ as a summand of $M$. [F2, F3, step 1.1, step 4.1]

6.1 If $M$ is indecomposable, step 5.1 gives $M\cong B_x(d)$. If two normalized candidates were obtained from different reduced expressions for $x$, applying that same splitting argument to either candidate makes them isomorphic, because their normalized rank-one top degrees force $d=0$. Distinct labels cannot be isomorphic, by their maximal support; distinct shifts at a fixed label cannot be isomorphic, by their top generator degrees. This proves classification and reduced-word independence. [step 3.1, step 5.1]

7.1 Restriction of degree-zero endomorphisms of $B_x$ to its rank-one top layer is a unital homomorphism onto $k$, since homogeneous scalars act there and its endomorphism ring in degree zero is $k$. Its kernel is a maximal ideal. Locality in step 1.1 makes this the unique maximal ideal, so the residue field is $k$. All selections were from finite supports and finite homogeneous bases, and no choice axiom beyond finite choice is used. The statement follows from steps 2.1, 3.1, 6.1 and this residue calculation. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 6.1] ∎

items.title: Normalized type-A Soergel bimodules are self-dual and have length degree bounds
items.statement: Over $k=\mathbb Q$ or $\mathbb R$, let $B_x$ be the normalized indecomposable bimodule classified by its top support. With right dual $DM=\operatorname{Hom}_{-R}^{\bullet}(M,R)$, one has $DB_x\cong B_x$. Its right reduction has degrees only in $[-\ell(x),\ell(x)]$, all congruent to $\ell(x)$ modulo two, and the two extremal dimensions are one. Hence its reduced graded dimensions are symmetric. Every Bott-Samelson word has a graded perfect symmetric invariant trace form. These assertions assume neither the Kazhdan-Lusztig character conjecture nor hard Lefschetz.
items.strategy:
1.1 The unit has the perfect multiplication form. If a right-free bimodule $M$ has an invariant form, put $a(b)=b c_{\mathrm{id}}$ and $b(b')=b'c_s$ in $MB_s$ and define the induced form by $\langle a(u),a(v)\rangle=\partial_s\langle u,v\rangle$, $\langle a(u),b(v)\rangle=\langle b(u),a(v)\rangle=\langle u,v\rangle$, and $\langle b(u),b(v)\rangle=\langle u,v\rangle\alpha_s$. Extend on a right basis by right bilinearity. The relation of [F2] and the identity $\partial_s(fr)=\partial_s(f)r+s(f)\partial_s(r)$ verify that these formulas agree for arbitrary $u,v$, and that left multiplication is self-adjoint. Symmetry follows from symmetry of the preceding form. If $e_i,e_i^*$ are dual right bases for that form, the pairing between bases $(a(e_i),b(e_i))$ and $(b(e_i^*),a(e_i^*))$ has matrix $\begin{pmatrix}I&0\\\alpha_sI&I\end{pmatrix}$, using $\partial_s(1)=0$, and has determinant one. Thus perfection is preserved. Iteration yields a perfect symmetric invariant form on every word, exactly its successive rank-one trace multiplication form. [given, F2, algebra]

2.1 For finite right-free modules the graded double-dual evaluation is an isomorphism, so $D$ is an involutive contravariant equivalence and takes indecomposables to indecomposables. The invariant perfect word form of step 1.1 identifies a word with its right dual. Generic graph support is unchanged by this duality: in a right basis left multiplication matrices transpose under $D$, so their simultaneous eigencharacters, and hence the graph labels after passing to the polynomial fraction field, are unchanged. A right-free summand has precisely the support closure of those graph labels. Therefore $DB_x$ is an indecomposable summand with the $x$ graph of the same reduced word. Uniqueness in [F1] identifies it with $B_x$ with no shift. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 A word of length $m$ has a homogeneous right basis given by tensor products of the two basis elements in [F2]; its generator degrees lie between $-m$ and $m$ and have parity $m$. Right reduction preserves a split direct-sum decomposition. Since $B_x$ is an unshifted summand of its reduced word of length $m=\ell(x)$, its reduction has these same bounds and parity. The word's bottom degree is the single $1$-tensor. The balanced evaluation of that word on its top graph, obtained by successively twisting the tensor-slot polynomials by the successive prefix permutations, sends this $1$-tensor to $1$. It factors through the rank-one top quotient, and is an isomorphism onto $R_x(m)$ because both generators have degree $-m$. All other summands have no $x$ support; consequently the projection of the bottom tensor into $B_x$ is nonzero. Its bottom dimension is therefore one. [F1, F2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Right duality reverses the degrees of the finite homogeneous basis after reduction. The unshifted duality $DB_x\cong B_x$ from step 2.1 therefore makes the reduced dimensions symmetric and gives top dimension one from the bottom dimension in step 3.1. The perfect trace forms, duality, degree bounds, parity and extremal dimensions have now all been established locally. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

items.title: The reduced Soergel module and the dominant Lefschetz operator
items.statement:
**The reduction.** Work over the ring $S=\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ of the real
scalar-extension definition ([[def-real-type-a-soergel-category-and-scalar-extension]]),
with $S_+=\bigoplus_{d>0}S_d$ the ideal of positive-degree elements; the residue
field of the right action is
$$k:=S/S_+=\mathbb R,$$
with quotient map $S\twoheadrightarrow k$, $s\mapsto \bar s$. For a graded
$(S,S)$-bimodule $M$ that is finite free as a right $S$-module put
$$\overline M:=M\otimes_Sk=M/MS_+,$$
the **reduction** of $M$: a finite-dimensional graded $k$-vector space, on which
the left $S$-action descends because $S_+\subseteq S$ is central and $MS_+$ is
stable under left multiplication. Write $\overline M^{\,i}$ for its homogeneous
component of degree $i$, $d_i(M):=\dim_{\mathbb R}\overline M^{\,i}$ for the
graded dimensions, and
$$\dim\overline M:=\sum_{i\in\mathbb Z}d_i(M)\,v^{-i}$$
for the **graded dimension** (a finite Laurent polynomial); all tensor products
below are over $S$. For a morphism $f:M\to M'$ of graded bimodules, i.e. a
degree-zero bi-$S$-linear map, the induced map
$$\overline f:\overline M\to\overline{M'},\qquad \overline f(m+MS_+):=f(m)+M'S_+ ,$$
is well defined and $k$-linear of degree zero, because $f(MS_+)\subseteq M'S_+$.
Reduction is a functor from finite right-free graded bimodules to finite
dimensional graded $k$-vector spaces; it preserves finite direct sums and
shifts, in the sense $\overline{M(d)}=\overline M(d)$ in the Elias-Williamson
shift convention $M(d)_e=M_{d+e}$.

**The dominant Lefschetz operator.** Fix a strictly dominant degree-two
element
$$\rho=\sum_{j=1}^nc_jx_j\in S_2,\qquad c_1>c_2>\cdots>c_n ,$$
which exists by [[def-real-type-a-soergel-category-and-scalar-extension]] (for
example $c_j=(n+1)/2-j$); recall that this is exactly the condition
$\rho(\alpha_i^\vee)>0$ for every simple coroot $\alpha_i^\vee$ in the
coordinate normalization of this page
([[def-finite-weyl-root-system-lattice-and-chamber-conventions]]). Let
$\rho\cdot(-):M\to M$, $m\mapsto\rho m$, denote left multiplication by $\rho$.
Since $S_+\subseteq S$ is central and $\rho\,(MS_+)\subseteq MS_+$, this
operator preserves the submodule $MS_+$ and therefore descends to a degree-two
$k$-linear endomorphism
$$L_0:=\rho\cdot(-):\overline M\longrightarrow\overline M,\qquad m+MS_+\longmapsto \rho m+MS_+,$$
called the **dominant Lefschetz operator** on $\overline M$. For rational
objects $B_x,B_s$ with real scalar extensions
$B_x^R=B_x\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb R$ and $B_s^R$, the same construction
applies to the reduced tensor product
$\overline{B_x^RB_s^R}=\overline{(B_xB_s)^R}$, where $B_xB_s$ denotes the
tensor product over the rational polynomial ring; the operator $L_0$ on it is
the value $\zeta=0$ of the deformed operator $L_\zeta$ defined later on this
page.

**Descent detection.** For every $w\in S_n$ and every simple reflection $s_i$
one has
$$(w\rho)(\alpha_i^\vee)>0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \ell(s_iw)>\ell(w).$$
Indeed, $(w\rho)(\alpha_i^\vee)=c_{w^{-1}(i)}-c_{w^{-1}(i+1)}$ is positive
exactly when $w^{-1}(i)<w^{-1}(i+1)$, the left-ascent criterion for inversion
length. Thus the displayed evaluation detects left descents; applied to
$w=x^{-1}$ it detects right descents of $x$, because $\ell(s_ix^{-1})=\ell(xs_i)$.

**Grading conventions.** The reduced module $\overline{B_x^R}$ has bottom degree
$-\ell(x)$ and top degree $+\ell(x)$; the unreduced bimodule has nonzero
components in arbitrarily high degrees. On a reduced module the "centered" degree $-i$ is the
internal degree $-i$, and the Lefschetz operator raises internal degree by two.
All homological (complex) shifts are written $[\,j\,]$ and all internal shifts
$(d)$, as on the rest of this page; the Bruhat order used throughout is the
rank-inequality order of
[[def-bruhat-order-on-the-symmetric-group]].
items.strategy: For a finite right-free bimodule M, reduction is M/(M S_+) and has finite graded dimension equal to its right rank. Left multiplication preserves this submodule and descends. In the coordinate normalization rho=Σ c_jx_j with c_1>...>c_n, (w rho)(alpha_i^vee)=c_{w^{-1}(i)}-c_{w^{-1}(i+1)}, positive exactly when w^{-1}(i)<w^{-1}(i+1), equivalently ell(s_iw)>ell(w). This elementary inversion criterion proves the stated sign identity directly, and with w=x^{-1} gives the positive coefficient (x^{-1}rho)(alpha_s^vee) when xs>x. The alternating balanced coroots of the diagrammatic presentation are not used in this criterion.

items.title: Indecomposable labels, characters and filtration ranks agree after real scalar extension
items.statement: Let $B_w$ be the rational indecomposable type-A Soergel bimodule and let $B_w^R$ be its real scalar extension. (1) $B_w^R$ is indecomposable; its finite-dimensional degree-zero endomorphism algebra is local with residue field $\mathbb R$. If $S(w)$ holds, its degree-zero endomorphism algebra is $\mathbb R$, but no rank-one assertion for the full graded endomorphism module is made. (2) Real extension preserves the labels and shifts of all finite Krull-Schmidt decompositions of rational Soergel bimodules, and every real indecomposable is a unique $B_w^R(d)$. (3) $\Delta$/$\nabla$ support-filtration multiplicities, characters, reduction by positive-degree right polynomials, and Hom spaces commute with scalar extension; thus character identities over $\mathbb R$ descend to $\mathbb Q$. (4) If $xs>x$ and $S(y)$ holds for all $y<xs$, then $B_xB_s=B_{xs}\oplus\bigoplus_{y<xs}B_y^{a_y}$ with $a_y$ nonnegative integers and no grading shifts; the top summand occurs once. If $xs<x$ and $S(x)$ holds, then $B_xB_s=B_x(1)\oplus B_x(-1)$. All assertions concern the normalized self-dual indecomposables.
items.strategy:
1.1 For finite right-free rational $M,N$, a homogeneous bimodule map is determined by the images of a finite right basis. In a fixed degree the finitely many left-generator commutation relations are finite linear equations with rational coefficients. Their kernel commutes with the flat field extension to $\mathbb R$. Thus every homogeneous Hom space, and its composition, commutes with extension. The support cut on a specified graph union is the common kernel of its finitely generated graph ideal acting on the carrier: the carrier is right-free and generically a sum of reduced graph modules, so the relations hold before localization by torsion-freeness. These kernels commute with flat extension as well. Therefore the canonical support submodules, quotients, graph generator degrees and multiplicities commute with extension. Right reduction commutes with it by tensor associativity and the augmentation map. [given, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 Let $A=\operatorname{End}^0(B_x)$ over $\mathbb Q$. By [F1] it is finite-dimensional local with residue $\mathbb Q$, and its maximal ideal $J$ is nilpotent by the finite-algebra proof there. Step 1.1 gives $\operatorname{End}^0(B_x^R)=A\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb R$. The ideal $J\otimes\mathbb R$ is nilpotent and its quotient is $\mathbb R$; an element with nonzero residue is invertible by a finite geometric series after subtracting its scalar part. Hence this algebra is local with residue $\mathbb R$, and $B_x^R$ is indecomposable. Its top support layer is unchanged by step 1.1, so the real classification [F1] identifies it with the same normalized real label. Every real word is the extension of its rational word and its rational finite decomposition; the real classification and uniqueness imply that all real indecomposables and all real decompositions are the corresponding labels and shifts. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Duality exchanges the $\Delta$ and $\nabla$ flags: dualize their right-split canonical layer sequences, which reverses order and the homogeneous degrees of their graph generators. A $\Delta_y(d)$ layer dualizes to $\nabla_y(-d)$. Therefore normalized self-duality gives $h_\Delta(B_y)=h_\nabla(B_y)$ by the weight conventions. The same is true for $B_xB_s$: an invariant isomorphism $B_x\to DB_x$ can be extended by the induced rank-one form construction in [F2], whose mixed-basis matrix has determinant one and yields an invariant isomorphism $B_xB_s\to D(B_xB_s)$. If $S(y)$ holds, both characters of $B_y$ are consequently $\underline H_y$. By [F3],[F4], its endomorphism Hom rank has no negative powers and constant term one. Since the polynomial ring has degree-zero part $\mathbb R$ and no negative degrees, its degree-zero endomorphism algebra is then exactly $\mathbb R$. [F2, F3, F4, step 2.1]

3.2 Step 1.1 proves the support multiplicity, character, Hom and reduction identities in (3). These characters have integer Laurent coefficients recording finite homogeneous graph bases; equality over the real category therefore gives the same integer coefficient equality over the rational category. No injectivity assertion about an unrelated extension of the coefficient ring is needed. [step 1.1, step 2.1]

3.3 For $xs>x$, assume $S(y)$ for every $y<xs$, including $x$. The tensor $M=B_xB_s$ is a summand of the reduced word for $xs$. Its top layer is the word's unique $\Delta_{xs}$, because the reduced word for $x$ decomposes as $B_x$ and lower-support summands, whose tensor with $B_s$ cannot reach length $\ell(xs)$. By [F1] its unique top summand is therefore $B_{xs}$ unshifted and once; the other summands are $B_y(d)$ with $y<xs$. This top-layer argument makes no substitution of the unknown character of $B_{xs}$. [F1, F2, F4, step 2.1]

4.1 The character of $M$ is $\underline H_x\underline H_s$, and its standard expansion lies in $\mathbb Z[v]$: the only $v^{-1}$ in simple multiplication multiplies a strictly lower coefficient already divisible by $v$, while the top coefficient is on an ascent. For every lower $y$, the two Hom ranks $\operatorname{Hom}(B_y,M)$ and $\operatorname{Hom}(M,B_y)$ are the standard pairings of this polynomial character with $\underline H_y$, using self-duality from step 3.1. Hence they have no negative powers, and both Hom spaces have no negative-degree maps. A summand $B_y(d)$ with $d>0$ gives a negative-degree inclusion from unshifted $B_y$, and one with $d<0$ gives a negative-degree projection to it, by the convention $M(d)_i=M_{i+d}$. Both are impossible. Thus every lower summand is unshifted, proving the ascent statement with its actual nonnegative multiplicities $a_y$. The character of the top summand is not yet required to equal $\underline H_{xs}$, and no equality $a_y=\mu(y,x)$ is inferred. [F3, F4, F5, step 3.1, step 3.3]

4.2 For $xs<x$ and $S(x)$, the support of $M=B_xB_s$ stays at most $x$: take a reduced word for $x$ ending in $s$; toggling its last letter shows that the graphs $y,ys$ for $y\le x$ stay in this Bruhat interval. Its character is $(v+v^{-1})\underline H_x$ by [F4],[F5], so its top $x$ layer has the two shifts $\Delta_x(1),\Delta_x(-1)$. The maximal-layer splitting proof of [F1] splits off exactly $B_x(1)$ and $B_x(-1)$. Under $S(x)$ their characters already sum to the whole character of $M$. Any remaining nonzero summand would have a nonzero graph layer with a positive integral multiplicity, contradicting its zero character. Thus $M=B_x(1)\oplus B_x(-1)$ with no other summands, without assuming $S$ for any other label. [F1, F4, F5, step 3.1]

5.1 The local algebra and real indecomposability are step 2.1, and the degree-zero scalar assertion under $S(x)$ is step 3.1. Step 2.1 proves classification after extension, step 3.2 proves all base-change identities, and steps 3.3–4.2 prove the two decompositions with their exact stated hypotheses. Normalization and self-duality come from [F2], proved before the character comparisons. [F2, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 3.2, step 4.1, step 4.2] ∎

items.title: The trace, the invariant intersection form on Bott-Samelson bimodules and its reduction
items.statement:
**The Bott-Samelson bimodule and its subexpression basis.** Fix a finite word
$\underline x=s_1\cdots s_m$ in the simple reflections and let
$$\mathrm{BS}(\underline x):=B_{s_1}\otimes_S\cdots\otimes_SB_{s_m}$$
be the real Bott-Samelson bimodule
([[def-bott-samelson-bimodule-of-a-word]]), with $B_s=S\otimes_{S^s}S(1)$
([[def-type-a-soergel-bimodule-for-a-simple-reflection]]). In each factor put
$$c_{\mathrm{id}}:=1\otimes1,\qquad c_s:=\tfrac12\bigl(\alpha_s\otimes1+1\otimes\alpha_s\bigr),$$
of degrees $-1$ and $+1$; here $\alpha_s$ is the coordinate root of
[[def-real-type-a-soergel-category-and-scalar-extension]], so that
$\partial_s(r)=(r-sr)/\alpha_s$ is the coordinate Demazure operator. The
elements $\{c_{\mathrm{id}},c_s\}$ form a right (and a left) $S$-basis of $B_s$
and the multiplication rules
$$c_{\mathrm{id}}c_{\mathrm{id}}=c_{\mathrm{id}},\qquad c_{\mathrm{id}}c_s=c_s,\qquad c_sc_s=c_s\alpha_s$$
hold. For a subexpression $\varepsilon=(\varepsilon_1,\ldots,\varepsilon_m)$
with $\varepsilon_i\in\{\mathrm{id},s_i\}$ put
$$c_\varepsilon:=c_{\varepsilon_1}\cdots c_{\varepsilon_m}\in\mathrm{BS}(\underline x),$$
the tensor product of the chosen elements, and put
$$c_{\mathrm{top}}:=c_{s_1}\cdots c_{s_m}.$$
The elements $\{c_\varepsilon\}$ form a right (and a left) $S$-basis of
$\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)$; the bimodule is finite free of rank $2^m$ on each
side ([[lem-type-a-soergel-generators-are-finite-free-on-both-sides]]).
Moreover $\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)\cong\bigl(S\otimes_{S^{s_1}}S\otimes_{S^{s_2}}\cdots\otimes_{S^{s_m}}S\bigr)(m)$,
so after the shift by $(-m)$ the termwise multiplication makes
$\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)(-m)$ a commutative ring with unit $c_{\mathrm{id}}\cdots c_{\mathrm{id}}$;
in particular it contains the powers of any degree-two element and products of
commuting elements.

**The trace and the intersection form.** Define the **trace**
$$\operatorname{Tr}:\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)\longrightarrow S$$
to be the coefficient of $c_{\mathrm{top}}$ when an element is written in the
right basis $\{c_\varepsilon\}$, and define the **intersection form** by
$$\langle b,b'\rangle:=\operatorname{Tr}(b\,b'),$$
the product being taken in the commutative ring $\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)(-m)$.
Then:

1. $\langle-,-\rangle$ is a graded symmetric form, $S$-bilinear for the right
   action, and invariant in the sense
   $\langle rb,b'\rangle=\langle b,rb'\rangle$ and
   $\langle br,b'\rangle=\langle b,b'r\rangle=\langle b,b'\rangle r$ for
   $r\in S$;
2. if $B$ is a direct summand of a finite direct sum of shifts of
   Bott-Samelson bimodules, then an invariant form on $B$ is obtained by
   restricting an invariant form of the ambient finite sum, and the restriction
   is determined up to the choices of the ambient forms;
3. for a self-dual bimodule $B$ with invariant form $\langle-,-\rangle_B$ the
   **induced form** on $BB_s$ is the unique invariant form satisfying, for all
   $b,b'\in B$,
   $$\langle\alpha(b),\alpha(b')\rangle=\partial_s(\langle b,b'\rangle_B),\qquad \langle\alpha(b),\beta(b')\rangle=\langle b,b'\rangle_B=\langle\beta(b),\alpha(b')\rangle,\qquad \langle\beta(b),\beta(b')\rangle=\langle b,b'\rangle_B\,\alpha_s,$$
   where $\alpha(b):=b\,c_{\mathrm{id}}$ and $\beta(b):=b\,c_s$;
4. the intersection form on a Bott-Samelson bimodule is non-degenerate as an
   $S$-valued form, and for a summand $B$ of a Bott-Samelson bimodule the
   restricted form is non-degenerate whenever $B$ has finite free right
   $S$-rank and the induced reduced form on $\overline B$ is non-degenerate
   (graded Nakayama);
5. the reduction of $\langle-,-\rangle$ is a graded symmetric $k$-valued form
   $\langle-,-\rangle_{\overline M}$ on $\overline M$
   ([[def-reduced-soergel-module-and-dominant-lefschetz-operator]]), and for a
   finite right-free $M$ the $S$-valued form is non-degenerate if and only if
   the reduced form is graded non-degenerate;
6. Bott-Samelson bimodules and the indecomposable bimodules $B_w^R$ are
   self-dual, so
   $\dim(\overline{B_w^R})^{-i}=\dim(\overline{B_w^R})^{i}$ for all $i$
   (symmetric Betti numbers).

Additionally record the left/right asymmetry: the form is bilinear for the
right action and satisfies the two invariance identities displayed in (1); it is
not left $S$-bilinear in general, because $\langle rb,b'\rangle$ is defined
through the trace of a product while the two $S$-actions differ on
$\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)$.
items.strategy: Items (1),(3) are direct computations in the commutative ring BS(x)(-m) and the multiplication rules c_id c_id = c_id, c_id c_s = c_s, c_s c_s = c_s alpha_s, using the identity Tr(chi_i gamma) = Tr_i(gamma); (2) is the induced-form calculation with the basis {alpha(e_i), beta(e_i)} and its dual; (4) is the determinant computation with the block matrix having identity diagonal blocks and the vanishing lower-left block (partial_s(1) = 0); (5) is the graded Nakayama lemma applied to the free right S-module together with the observation that an invariant form is the same as a bimodule map B -> DB. For (6), self-duality of Bott-Samelson bimodules follows from the explicit dual basis of the commutative presentation, and self-duality of B_w^R is a consequence of the base-change classification lemma proved on this page (the rational statement is part of the published type-A classification, and self-duality is preserved by the flat base change Q -> R).

items.title: Primitive subspaces, hard Lefschetz and the Hodge-Riemann signs: the dictionary of hypotheses S, hL and HR
items.statement:
**The linear-algebraic data.** Let $H=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb Z}H^i$ be a
finite-dimensional graded real vector space, concentrated in a single parity
(all nonzero $H^i$ have $i\equiv j\pmod 2$ for one $j\in\{0,1\}$), equipped with
a graded symmetric bilinear form $\langle-,-\rangle$: symmetric in the sense of
[[def-bilinear-symmetric-skew-and-alternating-forms]] and graded in the sense
$\langle a,b\rangle=0$ unless $\deg a+\deg b=0$, non-degenerate in the sense that
the induced map $H\to H^*$ is an isomorphism; definiteness, inertia and
signature are used in the sense of
[[def-definiteness-inertia-and-signature-data-over-the-reals]], and Sylvester's
law [[thm-sylvesters-law-of-inertia]] supplies the uniqueness of the inertia.
Let $L:H\to H$ be a **symmetric degree-two operator**, i.e. $L(H^i)\subseteq H^{i+2}$
and $\langle La,b\rangle=\langle a,Lb\rangle$ for all $a,b$.

**Hard Lefschetz.** The operator $L$ satisfies **hard Lefschetz** (hL) when
$$L^i:H^{-i}\longrightarrow H^i$$
is an isomorphism for every $i\ge0$. Define the **primitive subspaces**
$$P_L^{-i}:=\ker\bigl(L^{i+1}|_{H^{-i}}\bigr)\subseteq H^{-i}\qquad(i\ge0),$$
and the **Lefschetz forms**
$$(a,b)_L^{-i}:=\langle a,L^ib\rangle\qquad(a,b\in H^{-i},\ i\ge0).$$
Under hL the **primitive decomposition**
$$H=\bigoplus_{i\ge0}\bigoplus_{j=0}^{i}L^jP_L^{-i}$$
holds; it is proved in the primitive-decomposition lemma later on this page,
together with the non-degeneracy of the Lefschetz forms and the signature
formula for them.

**The Hodge-Riemann sign.** Assume $H\ne0$ and let $-d$ be its lowest nonzero
degree, so $H^{-d}\ne0$ and $H^i=0$ for $i<-d$. The **standard sign** at degree
$-i$ is $(-1)^{(d-i)/2}$; when $d-i$ is odd the primitive space $P_L^{-i}$ is
declared zero and the sign is not used. The pair $(H,L,\langle-,-\rangle)$
satisfies the **Hodge-Riemann bilinear relations with the standard sign**
(HR) when hL holds and the Lefschetz form $(a,b)_L^{-i}$ on $P_L^{-i}$ is
definite of sign $(-1)^{(d-i)/2}$ for every $i\ge0$, with the bottom space
$P_L^{-d}=H^{-d}$ positive definite. **HR with global sign** $\varepsilon\in\{\pm1\}$
means that the same statement holds with $(-1)^{(d-i)/2}$ replaced by
$\varepsilon(-1)^{(d-i)/2}$; the standard sign is thus the normalization that
makes the bottom form positive.

**The hypotheses S, hL, HR for Soergel bimodules.** For $x\in S_n$ let
$B_x^R$ be the indecomposable real Soergel bimodule with its reduced module
$\overline{B_x^R}$ ([[def-reduced-soergel-module-and-dominant-lefschetz-operator]]).
The statement
$$\mathrm{S}(x):\qquad \operatorname{ch}(B_x^R)=\underline H_x$$
means that the character of $B_x^R$ is the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis element
$\underline H_x$ in the Hecke algebra of the type-A page. On $\overline{B_x^R}$
use the centered grading, the operator
$$L:=\rho\cdot(-)$$
of left multiplication by a strictly dominant $\rho$ as in
[[def-reduced-soergel-module-and-dominant-lefschetz-operator]], and the
**positively normalized intrinsic invariant form when $\mathrm{S}(x)$ holds**: the unique-up-to-scalar
non-degenerate invariant form of
[[def-invariant-intersection-form-on-a-bott-samelson-bimodule]], normalized so
that the bottom Lefschetz form $\langle\rho^{\ell(x)}c_{\mathrm{bot}},c_{\mathrm{bot}}\rangle$
on the one-dimensional space $\overline{B_x^R}^{-\ell(x)}$ equals $+1$. Here $d=\ell(x)$ by the proved normalized degree bounds. The property $\mathrm{hL}(x)$ always denotes hard Lefschetz for this operator on $\overline{B_x^R}$, independently of $\mathrm{S}(x)$. $\mathrm{HR}(x)$ denotes the conjunction of $\mathrm{S}(x)$ and the Hodge-Riemann relations with the standard sign for this normalized intrinsic form; its existence and uniqueness, and the nonzero positive bottom value used for normalization, are proved in [[lem-invariant-forms-on-soergel-bimodules-are-unique-up-to-scalar-and-nondegenerate]]. The **embedded-form statements**
refer to a reduced expression $\underline x$ of $x$ and an embedding
$B_x^R\subseteq\!\!\bigoplus\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)$ as a direct summand: then
$\mathrm{HRbar}(x)$ requires the general Hodge-Riemann relations above for the restricted intersection form through every such embedding, and its equivalence with
$\mathrm{HR}(x)$ (the comparison scalar is positive) is the content of the
invariant-form uniqueness lemma later on this page. The strong embedded-form
statement $\mathrm{HRbar}(x)$ is formulated for the restricted forms and makes
sense without assuming $\mathrm{S}(x)$.

**The ascent and deformation packages.** Fix $xs>x$ and put
$M=B_x^RB_s^R$, whose reduced module has lowest degree $-\ell(x)-1$; the ascent
packages are read with
$$d=\ell(x)+1,\qquad L=L_0\ \text{or}\ L_\zeta,$$
and inherit hL, HR, HRbar, and the sign $(-1)^{(\ell(x)+1-i)/2}$ from the
general definition above, where $L_\zeta$ is the deformed Lefschetz operator
defined later on this page. Thus $\mathrm{hL}(x,s)$, $\mathrm{HR}(x,s)$ refer to
a fixed reduced-word induced form on $M$, while $\mathrm{HRbar}(x,s)$ requires
the statement for every choice of reduced-word embeddings and induced forms;
the subscript $\zeta$ denotes the same statements for $L_\zeta$. The local
sign hypotheses $\mathrm{S}^\pm(y,x,s)$ concern the local intersection form
$(-,-)^{x,s}_y$ on $\operatorname{Hom}^0(B_y,M)$ defined later on this page:
$\mathrm{S}^+(y,x,s)$ means $(-1)^{(\ell(x)+1-\ell(y))/2}$-definiteness of that
form and $\mathrm{S}^-(y,x,s)$ the opposite definiteness, with the parity
convention of the primitive subspaces.

**Orthogonal sums.** If $H=\bigoplus_\alpha H_\alpha$ is an orthogonal direct
sum of $L$-stable graded subspaces and $H$ has lowest degree $-d$, then HR holds
for $(H,L,\langle-,-\rangle)$ if and only if each summand satisfies hL and its
primitive Lefschetz forms are definite with the **ambient** signs
$(-1)^{(d-i)/2}$; these need not be the summand's own standard signs when the
summands have different lowest degrees. The sign bookkeeping for orthogonal
blocks is used in the tensoring lemma of this page.
items.strategy: This fixes the centered grading and standard-sign normalization. The sign on primitives in degree -i is (-1)^{(d-i)/2}; it is positive at i=d and alternates every two degrees upward. For an indecomposable of length ell it equals (-1)^{(ell-i)/2}=(-1)^{(i-ell)/2}, precisely EW Theorem 1.4. For the tensor product in an ascent replace ell by ell(x)+1. The parity-only formula epsilon(-1)^{(-i+j)/2}, j=0 or 1, is equivalent after choosing epsilon to make the bottom form positive, and is not imposed simultaneously without that factor. Substantive primitive decomposition and form-normalization equivalences are proved by the named local lemmas. Orthogonal blocks use the common ambient signs; the tensoring lemma computes the necessary scalar signs explicitly.

items.title: Minimal complexes and the perverse truncations in the real type-A Soergel category
items.statement:
**The category and its radical.** Let $\mathcal B=\mathrm{SBim}_n^R$ be the real
graded type-A Soergel category of
[[def-real-type-a-soergel-category-and-scalar-extension]], with degree-zero
morphisms; it is a graded additive idempotent-complete category
([[def-additive-category]], [[def-the-idempotent-completion-of-a-preadditive-category]])
whose objects are finite direct sums of shifts of the indecomposables $B_w^R$
([[lem-rational-and-real-type-a-soergel-characters-and-indecomposable-labels-agree]]).
Its **categorical radical** is the two-sided ideal
$$\operatorname{rad}\mathcal B:=\{f:M\to N\ :\ \text{for every }g:N\to M,\ 1_M-gf\text{ is invertible}\},$$
and $q:\mathcal B\to\mathcal B^{ss}:=\mathcal B/\operatorname{rad}\mathcal B$ is
the quotient functor. The radical is defined by the displayed invertibility
criterion and is not claimed to be nilpotent in general; on objects with local
endomorphism rings (as here, by the comparison lemma) it consists of the
non-units in the relevant endomorphism algebras.

**Minimal complexes.** Let $K^b(\mathcal B)$ be the homotopy category of bounded
cochain complexes of graded bimodules with degree-zero differentials
([[def-bounded-complex-of-graded-bimodules-and-signed-tensor-totalization]],
[[def-homotopy-category-of-chain-complexes]]). A bounded complex $F$ is
**minimal** when $q(d_F)=0$ in every degree, i.e. every differential of $F$
lies in the radical. Homological shifts are written $[j]$
([[def-shift-of-a-chain-complex]]); mapping cones are as in
[[def-mapping-cone-of-a-chain-map]]; contractibility and homotopies are as in
[[def-complex-homotopy-and-contractibility-in-an-additive-category]]; and the
two-term cancellation used on this page is
[[thm-homological-gaussian-elimination-splits-off-a-contractible-two-term-complex]]
with the block calculus of
[[def-invertible-differential-block-and-schur-complement-reduction]].

**Perverse bimodules.** Let $\underline H_x$ be the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis of the
Hecke algebra of the frontier Hecke page, transported to this page by the
comparison lemma. A Soergel bimodule is **perverse** when its character is a
nonnegative integer combination of the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis elements
$\underline H_x$ (not of the standard basis elements $H_x$); it is
**p-split** when its indecomposable summands are shifts of perverse ones. Thus
if $\mathrm{S}(x)$ holds then $B_x^R$ is perverse, since its character is
$\underline H_x$; no other perversity of a normalized indecomposable is asserted
before $\mathrm{S}(x)$.

**The perverse cuts.** Let $M$ be p-split and fix a decomposition
$$M=\bigoplus_{x,k}B_x^R(k)^{m_{x,k}}$$
with the normalized $B_x^R$ perverse (such a decomposition exists by the
comparison lemma, and the cuts below are proved intrinsic by the structural
lemma). For $j\in\mathbb Z$ set
$$\tau_{\le j}M:=\bigoplus_{k\ge -j}B_x^R(k)^{m_{x,k}},\qquad \tau_{<j}M:=\tau_{\le j-1}M,\qquad \tau_{\ge j}M:=M/\tau_{<j}M,$$
and define the associated graded
$$H^j(M):=\bigl(\tau_{\le j}M/\tau_{<j}M\bigr)(j),$$
so that the $j$-th perverse piece is normalized by the internal shift $(j)$.
Internal shifts $(d)$ change module degrees and homological shifts $[j]$ change
complex degrees; the two are kept distinct throughout.

**The perverse subcategories of complexes.** For a bounded complex
$F=(F^i,d^i)$ define
$$F\in pK^b_{\ge0}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad F\ \text{is isomorphic in }K^b(\mathcal B)\ \text{to a complex with p-split terms and}\ \tau_{<-i}(F^i)=0\ \text{for all }i,$$
$$F\in pK^b_{\le0}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad F\ \text{is isomorphic in }K^b(\mathcal B)\ \text{to a complex with p-split terms and}\ F^i=\tau_{\le-i}(F^i)\ \text{for all }i.$$
Equivalently, in the termwise decompositions the internal shifts $k$ satisfy
$k\le i$ for $pK^b_{\ge0}$ and $k\ge i$ for $pK^b_{\le0}$. The structural lemma
of this page supplies the semisimplicity of $\mathcal B^{ss}$, the existence and
uniqueness of minimal models, the intrinsicness and functoriality of the cuts,
their preservation under direct summands and their extension closure in
distinguished triangles; none of these properties is asserted by this
definition. The objects $pK^b_{\ge0}$ and $pK^b_{\le0}$ are the classes inside
which the Rouquier complexes of the next items are shown to lie, following the
orientation of Elias-Williamson Section 6.3.
items.strategy: Define the radical by the invertibility criterion and the minimal/perverse objects by the displayed conditions. The structural lemma proves their claimed well-definedness and model-independent properties; do not assert radical zero for a normalized indecomposable before S(x).

items.title: The Lefschetz operator factors through deleted Bott-Samelson subwords, with positive rescalings
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct; a rank-one computation followed by iteration over the letters.

1.1 **The single-factor identity.** Let $s$ be a simple reflection with root $\alpha=\alpha_s$, let $\mathrm{Br}(b):=bc_s$ on $B_s$, and let $\sigma\in S$. For every $b\in B_s$ one has $\sigma\cdot b=b\cdot(s\sigma)+\partial_s(\sigma)\,\mathrm{Br}(b)$. Indeed both sides are right $S$-linear in $b$, so it suffices to check the two basis elements: for $b=c_{\mathrm{id}}$ the identity is the rule $r\cdot c_{\mathrm{id}}=c_{\mathrm{id}}\cdot sr+\partial_s(r)c_s$ of [F1] with $r=\sigma$, and for $b=c_s$ it reads $\sigma\cdot c_s=c_s\cdot s\sigma+\partial_s(\sigma)c_s\alpha_s$, which is $c_s\sigma=c_s(s\sigma+\alpha_s\partial_s(\sigma))$ and holds because $\sigma-s\sigma=\alpha_s\partial_s(\sigma)$ and $c_s$ commutes with $S$. [given, F1]

2.1 **Iteration over the letters proves (a).** For $m=0$ both outer actions are multiplication by $\rho$ on $S$. For $m>0$, put $\sigma_0=\rho$ and $\sigma_i=s_i\sigma_{i-1}$. Apply step 1.1 in slot $i$ to the remainder $b_1\cdots b_{i-1}(\sigma_{i-1}b_i)b_{i+1}\cdots b_m$. This produces $\partial_{s_i}(\sigma_{i-1})\mathrm{Br}_i(b)$ and a remainder with $\sigma_i$ acting on the right of slot $i$. Balancing moves that polynomial to the left of slot $i+1$; at the last slot it is the outer right action by $x^{-1}\rho$. Each $\sigma_{i-1}$ is linear, so $\partial_{s_i}(\sigma_{i-1})=\sigma_{i-1}(\alpha_{s_i}^\vee)=\gamma_i$. Also $bc_s=\mu(b)c_s$ in one factor: on $c_{\mathrm{id}}$ and $c_s$ this follows from $\mu(c_{\mathrm{id}})=1$, $\mu(c_s)=\alpha_s$ and $c_s^2=c_s\alpha_s$. Thus $\mathrm{Br}_i=\chi_i\varphi_i$ with the appropriate shift of $\chi_i$, and the stated degree-two identity holds on every tensor monomial and hence on the whole bimodule. [step 1.1, F1]

3.1 **The covariance identity.** For all $b,b'\in\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)$ and all $i$ one has $\langle b,\mathrm{Br}_i b'\rangle=\langle\varphi_ib,\varphi_ib'\rangle_i$. It suffices to check on tensor monomials $b=b_1\cdots b_m$, $b'=b'_1\cdots b'_m$: the left side is $\operatorname{Tr}\bigl((b_1b'_1)\cdots(b_ib'_ic_{s_i})\cdots(b_mb'_m)\bigr)=\operatorname{Tr}\bigl((b_1b'_1)\cdots\mu(b_i)\mu(b'_i)c_{s_i}\cdots(b_mb'_m)\bigr)$, using $b_ic_{s_i}=\mu(b_i)c_{s_i}$ from step 2.1, so this equals $\operatorname{Tr}\bigl(\chi_i((b_1b'_1)\cdots\mu(b_i)\mu(b'_i)\cdots(b_mb'_m))\bigr)=\operatorname{Tr}_i((b_1b'_1)\cdots\mu(b_i)\mu(b'_i)\cdots(b_mb'_m))=\langle\varphi_ib,\varphi_ib'\rangle_i$, using $\operatorname{Tr}\circ\chi_i=\operatorname{Tr}_i$ and the multiplicativity of the ring structure. [step 1.1, step 2.1, given, F1]

4.1 **The rescaled form identity (b).** With $\varphi=\sum_i\varphi_i$ and $\langle-,-\rangle'=\bigoplus_i\langle-,-\rangle_i'$, the direct sum decomposition is orthogonal, so for all $b,b'$ one has $\langle\varphi(b),\varphi(b')\rangle'=\sum_i\gamma_i\langle b,\mathrm{Br}_ib'\rangle$; substituting step 3.1 gives $\sum_i\gamma_i\langle b,\mathrm{Br}_ib'\rangle=\langle b,\sum_i\gamma_i\mathrm{Br}_ib'\rangle$, and substituting the factorization of step 2.1 gives $\langle b,\rho b'\rangle-\langle b,b'\cdot x^{-1}\rho\rangle$. The second summand is $-\langle b,b'\rangle\,x^{-1}\rho$ by right $S$-linearity of the form, and it vanishes after reduction because $x^{-1}\rho$ has positive degree; hence $\langle b,\rho b'\rangle_{\overline{\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)}}=\langle\varphi(b),\varphi(b')\rangle'$ for $b,b'$ in the reduced module, as claimed in (b). [step 2.1, step 3.1, F1, algebra]

5.1 **Positivity for reduced words and the vanished remainder (c).** Let $\underline x$ be reduced. For each $i$, the prefix $w_i:=s_{i-1}\cdots s_1$ has length $i-1$ and $s_iw_i$ has length $i$; the descent criterion [F3] therefore gives $\gamma_i=(w_i\rho)(\alpha_{s_i}^\vee)>0$. All rescalings are by strictly positive real numbers, so no sign in a definite form changes; and the polynomial $x^{-1}\rho$ lies in $S_2\subset S_+$ whose right multiplication lands in $\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)S_+$, which becomes zero after reduction, so the remainder vanishes on the reduced module. This proves (c). [step 4.1, F1, F2, F3]

6.1 **Identification with the Rouquier differential (d).** By [F4] the first differential of the Rouquier complex is the sum, over the letters, of the maps $\varphi_i$ from the cohomological degree $0$ term $\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)$ to the degree $1$ term $\bigoplus_i\mathrm{BS}(\widehat{\underline x}_i)(1)$, and its dual maps decompose the generator $c_{s_i}$ back, i.e. are the maps $\chi_i$ with the displayed internal shifts. Composing the differential with the rescaled dual maps $\gamma_i\chi_i$ and summing over $i$ gives $\sum_i\gamma_i\mathrm{Br}_i$, which by step 2.1 equals left multiplication by $\rho$ modulo the right-multiplication remainder that vanishes on the reduced module by step 5.1. Hence left multiplication by $\rho$ on the reduced Bott-Samelson module factors, up to the positive rescalings $\gamma_i$, as the composite $\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)\xrightarrow{\varphi}\bigoplus_i\mathrm{BS}(\widehat{\underline x}_i)(1)\xrightarrow{\ \gamma\chi\ }\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)(2)$ built from the first Rouquier differential and its dual; all first-differential Koszul signs are $+1$, because every preceding tensor factor is in cohomological degree zero, so this is exactly $\rho\cdot(-)$ after right reduction. This proves (d) and completes the lemma; no positivity of characters and no character conjecture is used. [step 2.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, F2, F4] ∎

items.title: Invariant forms on an indecomposable Soergel bimodule are unique up to scalar, non-degenerate, and agree with the restricted Bott-Samelson form
items.strategy:
1.1 First prove the missing reduced-word bottom positivity. For a reduced word of length $m$, the bottom line is its $1$-tensor and the top line its all-$c_s$ tensor. Induct on $m$, with value $1$ for the empty word. The factorization in [F3] gives $\rho c_{\mathrm{bot}}=\sum_i\gamma_i\chi_i(c_{\mathrm{bot}})$ after reduction. If the deleted word is reduced, applying $\rho^{m-1}$ and induction gives a positive multiple $N_i c_{\mathrm{top}}$. If it is not reduced, every indecomposable in its finite decomposition has label of length less than $m-1$, by the subexpression support and classification. On every shift of such a summand, $\rho^{m-1}$ vanishes by the degree span in [F3], so this deletion contributes zero. At least the last deletion is reduced. Thus $\rho^m c_{\mathrm{bot}}=(\sum_{i\text{ reduced deletion}}\gamma_iN_i)c_{\mathrm{top}}$ with positive coefficient. The trace of $c_{\mathrm{top}}$ is one, proving the positive bottom Lefschetz value without assuming hard Lefschetz. [F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 Under $S(x)$ the unshifted duality and degree-zero endomorphism computation of [F2] give a one-dimensional space $\operatorname{Hom}^0(B_x,DB_x)$ which contains an isomorphism. Every nonzero map in this space is consequently an isomorphism, proving (1) directly. For an arbitrary embedding into a reduced word, the normalized bottom line of $B_x$ maps isomorphically to the word's bottom line by the degree bounds. Step 1.1 therefore makes the restricted invariant symmetric form nonzero; by this one-dimensional argument it is perfect. Normalize one such form to bottom value one. Every embedding's restriction is then a positive scalar multiple, proving (2) without inferring perfection merely from an ambient perfect form. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1]

3.1 Positive scalar multiples have the same primitive spaces, because the operator is unchanged, and their Lefschetz forms have the same definiteness signs. Hence the intrinsic standard-sign HR condition under $S(x)$ is equivalent to the restricted-form condition for every embedding, and already to that for any one embedding. This proves (3), with the conditional intrinsic form and unconditional embedded-form convention of [F4]. [F4, step 2.1]

3.2 For labels $y\ne z$ with $S(y),S(z)$, the actual graded Hom formula and the standard KL trace pairing give $\operatorname{Hom}^0(B_y,DB_z)=0$: its free Hom rank lies in $v\mathbb Z[v]$, and the polynomial ring has no negative degrees. This is a degree-zero Hom calculation, rather than an inference from the locality of their endomorphism rings. Thus every invariant form on $\bigoplus_zB_z^{m_z}$ pairs different isotypic components orthogonally. On one component, each matrix entry is a scalar multiple of the fixed perfect normalized $B_z$ form by (1), giving exactly a multiplicity-space matrix $Q_z$. Symmetry of the full form is symmetry of $Q_z$, and perfection is nonsingularity of every $Q_z$. Orthogonal diagonalization of each finite real symmetric matrix, or the elimination proof of [F5], supplies the claimed orthogonal copies and proves (4). No assertion that different multiplicity matrices are scalar multiples is made. [F1, F2, F5, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Step 2.1 proves uniqueness, perfection and positive comparison, step 3.1 the HR equivalence, and step 3.2 the complete isotypic multiplicity description. The bottom calculation was proved first in step 1.1 from normalized degree bounds and positive factorization, and no character theorem for the next label or Hodge conclusion was assumed. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 3.2] ∎

items.title: Hard Lefschetz gives the primitive decomposition, orthogonality and the signature formula
items.statement:
Let $H$ have a graded non-degenerate symmetric form and a symmetric degree-two operator $L$.

(a) If hL holds then $H=\bigoplus_{i\ge0}\bigoplus_{j=0}^{i}L^jP_L^{-i}$; more precisely, in each degree $-i$ one has $H^{-i}=\bigoplus_{k\ge0}L^kP_L^{-(i+2k)}$.

(b) In each degree $-i$, the decomposition of (a) is orthogonal for the Lefschetz form $\langle a,L^ib\rangle$.

(c) All Lefschetz forms on $H^{-i}$ are non-degenerate exactly when hL holds.

(d) If $H$ has one parity and lowest degree $-d$, standard HR is equivalent to hL together with the signature formula $\operatorname{sig}\bigl(\langle-,L^i-\rangle|_{H^{-i}}\bigr)=\sum_{k\ge0}(-1)^{(d-i-2k)/2}\dim P_L^{-(i+2k)}$ for every $i\ge0$ (zero spaces omitted).

(e) If $H$ satisfies hL, an $L$-stable graded subspace $V\subseteq H$ with $\dim V^{-i}=\dim V^i$ for all $i$ inherits hL; if $H$ satisfies HR then the restricted form on $V$ is non-degenerate and $V$ inherits the ambient primitive signs, and its standard global sign agrees with that of $H$ when their lowest degrees coincide.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct; primitive-string decomposition and orthogonal signature bookkeeping.

1.1 **One step of the decomposition.** Under hL the map $L^{i+2}:H^{-i-2}\to H^{i+2}$ is an isomorphism, so for every $a\in H^{-i}$ there is $b\in H^{-i-2}$ with $L^{i+1}a=L^{i+2}b$; then $a-Lb\in P_L^{-i}$, and hence $H^{-i}=P_L^{-i}+L\,H^{-i-2}$. The sum is direct: if $Lb\in P_L^{-i}$, then $0=L^{i+1}(Lb)=L^{i+2}b$ and injectivity of $L^{i+2}$ gives $b=0$; hence $H^{-i}=P_L^{-i}\oplus L\,H^{-i-2}$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 **Iteration and the primitive decomposition (a).** Iterating step 1.1 gives $H^{-i}=P_L^{-i}\oplus L\,P_L^{-i-2}\oplus L^2P_L^{-i-4}\oplus\cdots=\bigoplus_{k\ge0}L^kP_L^{-(i+2k)}$, the sum terminating because $H^{-m}=0$ for $m>d$; For positive degree $i$, hL gives $H^i=L^iH^{-i}$, so applying $L^i$ to the negative-degree decomposition supplies all positive pieces. Reindexing by the lowest primitive degree gives $H=\bigoplus_{i\ge0}\bigoplus_{j=0}^{i}L^jP_L^{-i}$, since every string $L^kP_L^{-i}$ lies in degrees between $-i$ and $i$, so $k\le i$ for nonzero contributions. This proves (a). [step 1.1, F1]

3.1 **Orthogonality (b).** Let $p\in P_L^{-(i+2k)}$ and $q\in P_L^{-(i+2l)}$ with $k<l$ and consider $a=L^kp$, $b=L^lq$ in $H^{-i}$. Using symmetry of $L$ repeatedly, $(a,b)_L^{-i}=\langle L^kp,L^{i+l}q\rangle=\langle p,L^{i+k+l}q\rangle$, and the exponent satisfies $i+k+l\ge i+2k+1$; since $L^{i+2k+1}p=0$, the pairing vanishes. Hence distinct strings are orthogonal for the Lefschetz form, as claimed. [step 2.1, F1, F4, algebra]

4.1 **Non-degeneracy of the Lefschetz forms is equivalent to hL (c).** For fixed $i$, the Lefschetz form at degree $-i$ is the composite of the linear map $L^i:H^{-i}\to H^i$ with the perfect pairing $H^i\times H^{-i}\to\mathbb R$ given by the form; the latter is an isomorphism $H^i\to(H^{-i})^*$ by non-degeneracy of $\langle-,-\rangle$ [F1]. Hence the Lefschetz form is non-degenerate if and only if $L^i$ is an isomorphism; this holds simultaneously for all $i\ge0$ exactly when hL holds, and for $i>d$ both sides are zero by [F1] ($\dim H^i=\dim H^{-i}=0$). This proves (c). [step 3.1, F1, F3]

5.1 **Signature formula (d).** Assume hL and the standard-sign definiteness on primitives. The orthogonal decomposition of step 3.1 expresses the form on $H^{-i}$ as an orthogonal sum of the forms $(p,q)\mapsto\langle p,L^{i+2k}q\rangle$ on the primitive spaces $P_L^{-(i+2k)}$; each of these is definite of sign $(-1)^{(d-i-2k)/2}$ by HR, and its own inertia is therefore $(\dim P,0,0)$ or $(0,\dim P,0)$ according to that sign. Sylvester's law [F2] makes the signature of the orthogonal sum the sum of the summand signatures, giving the displayed formula. Conversely, assume hL and the signature formula for all $i$; descending from the bottom degree, the formula determines the signature of the primitive form on $P_L^{-(i+2k)}$ after the signatures of the higher-degree primitive spaces are known, the orthogonal decomposition and step 4.1 make each primitive form non-degenerate, and the subtraction forces its signature to be the prescribed sign times its dimension. Its inertia therefore has only positive or only negative entries by [F2], so each primitive form is definite with the stated sign; this recovers HR. This proves (d). [step 3.1, step 4.1, F2]

6.1 **Stable subspaces (e).** Let $V\subseteq H$ be $L$-stable with $\dim V^{-i}=\dim V^i$. Since $L^i$ is injective on $H$ (hL), its restriction to $V$ is injective, and the dimension symmetry makes it an isomorphism onto $V^i$; hence $V$ satisfies hL for the restricted operator and form. Its primitive spaces are $P_V^{-i}=V^{-i}\cap P_L^{-i}$, because the kernel of $L^{i+1}$ on $V^{-i}$ is the intersection with the kernel on $H^{-i}$; the restricted Lefschetz form on $P_V^{-i}$ is the restriction of the ambient definite primitive form, hence definite with the ambient sign $(-1)^{(d-i)/2}$. The string construction in steps 1.1–2.1 uses only hL, so it applies to $V$ before non-degeneracy of its restricted form is known. This primitive decomposition then shows, exactly as in step 5.1, that the restricted form on $V$ is an orthogonal sum of definite blocks, hence non-degenerate, and that its signs are the ambient signs; if the lowest nonzero degree of $V$ equals $-d$, then the ambient sign formula is also the standard sign of $V$. This proves (e) and completes the lemma. [step 2.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, F1, F2] ∎

items.title: The deformed Lefschetz operator L_zeta on B_x B_s
items.statement:
**The operator.** Fix $x\in S_n$, a simple reflection $s$, a strictly dominant
$\rho\in S_2$ ([[def-reduced-soergel-module-and-dominant-lefschetz-operator]])
and a real parameter $\zeta\ge0$. On the tensor product
$B_x^RB_s^R=B_x^R\otimes_SB_s^R$ define
$$L_\zeta:=(\rho\cdot(-))\otimes\mathrm{id}_{B_s^R}+\mathrm{id}_{B_x^R}\otimes(\zeta\,\rho\cdot(-)),$$
where the first summand is left multiplication by $\rho$ on the first factor and
the second summand is left multiplication by $\zeta\rho$ on the second factor.
Because the polynomial ring is commutative and the balanced tensor product
identifies $b r\otimes c=b\otimes rc$ for $r\in S$, the second summand equals
right multiplication by $\zeta\rho$ on the first factor; both summands are
degree-two, $S$-linear on the right, and commute, so $L_\zeta$ is a degree-two
right-$S$-linear endomorphism of $B_x^RB_s^R$. In particular $L_\zeta$ preserves
the submodule $MS_+$ for $M=B_x^RB_s^R$ and therefore descends to a degree-two
$\mathbb R$-linear endomorphism of the reduced module
$\overline{B_x^RB_s^R}$ ([[def-invariant-intersection-form-on-a-bott-samelson-bimodule]]
supplies the induced invariant form and the reduction conventions of
[[def-reduced-soergel-module-and-dominant-lefschetz-operator]] apply).

**Symmetry.** Each summand of $L_\zeta$ is multiplication by an element in the
commutative position algebra of the tensor product: the first is multiplication
by $\rho$ on the first factor, the second is right (equivalently middle)
multiplication by $\zeta\rho$, which is self-adjoint for the induced invariant
form by the invariance identities of the form. Hence $L_\zeta$ is symmetric for
the induced form, and the Lefschetz forms $(\ ,\ )^{-i}_{L_\zeta}$ and the
primitive subspaces $P^{-i}_{L_\zeta}$ are those of
[[def-primitive-subspaces-hard-lefschetz-and-hodge-riemann-signs]] for this
operator.

**The deformation statements.** Write $\mathrm{hL}(x,s)_\zeta$,
$\mathrm{HR}(x,s)_\zeta$ and $\mathrm{HRbar}(x,s)_\zeta$ for centered hard
Lefschetz, the Hodge-Riemann relations and the strong embedded-form statement on
$\overline{B_x^RB_s^R}$ for the operator $L_\zeta$, with the bottom degree
$-\ell(x)-1$ and the standard sign
$(-1)^{(\ell(x)+1-i)/2}$ of the dictionary in
[[def-primitive-subspaces-hard-lefschetz-and-hodge-riemann-signs]]; the
definitions of $\mathrm{HR}(x,s)_\zeta$ and $\mathrm{HRbar}(x,s)_\zeta$ refer to
a fixed reduced-word induced form respectively to all choices of such forms.
At $\zeta=0$ the operator $L_0=\rho\cdot(-)\otimes\mathrm{id}$ is left
multiplication by $\rho$ on the first factor, so the zero-parameter statements
$\mathrm{hL}(x,s)_0$, $\mathrm{HR}(x,s)_0$, $\mathrm{HRbar}(x,s)_0$ are exactly
the undeformed statements $\mathrm{hL}(x,s)$, $\mathrm{HR}(x,s)$,
$\mathrm{HRbar}(x,s)$ of the dictionary. For fixed data the family
$\zeta\mapsto L_\zeta$ is polynomial of degree one in $\zeta$.

**Summand stability.** Any direct summand $B\subseteq B_x^RB_s^R$ that is a
sub-bimodule is stable under $L_0$, because left multiplication by the central
element $\rho$ is a bimodule endomorphism; stability under $L_\zeta$ for
$\zeta>0$ is a separate condition, since a projector onto $B$ need not commute
with the middle-position operator. The undeformed summand implications used in
the induction of this page are supplied by the local restriction lemma later on
this page, after deforming the parameter back to $\zeta=0$; no statement of this
definition identifies a restricted positive-parameter operator with a
restriction of $L_\zeta$.

All terms are right-linear, so preserve the right augmentation ideal. Invariance of the form proves symmetry separately for left multiplication on the first tensor factor and left multiplication on the second factor. The identities at zero and polynomial dependence are direct calculations. Do not infer hL(xs) or HR(xs) by restricting L_zeta to a chosen bimodule summand at positive zeta; use the separately proved undeformed restriction lemma.

items.title: Radical quotients, minimal complexes and perverse filtrations in the Soergel category
items.statement:
(1) The quotient $\mathcal B^{ss}$ is semisimple with simple classes $B_x(k)$ and endomorphism rings $\mathbb R$, and $q$ reflects isomorphisms.

(2) Every bounded complex of $\mathcal B$ has a minimal direct summand whose inclusion is a homotopy equivalence, and any two minimal models are isomorphic as complexes.

(3) Every direct summand of a perverse (respectively p-split) bimodule is perverse (respectively p-split).

(4) For perverse $M,N$ one has $\operatorname{Hom}(M,N(-i))=0$ for $i>0$.

(5) The perverse cuts on p-split bimodules are independent of the chosen decomposition and are preserved by every morphism.

(6) The definitions of $pK^b_{\ge0}$ and $pK^b_{\le0}$ can equivalently be tested on the minimal model, and both classes are closed under extensions in distinguished triangles.
items.strategy:
1.1 In finite decompositions, the categorical radical consists of arbitrary maps between different indecomposable classes and, between copies of the same class, matrices whose every entry belongs to that class's local maximal ideal. Indeed a composite through a different indecomposable class cannot be a unit on an indecomposable, since a unit composite would split an inclusion and make those classes isomorphic. Hence these matrices form an ideal, and the quotient is the product of full matrix algebras over the residue fields $\mathbb R$ of [F1]. This uses the whole repeated-class matrix, not just its diagonal entries. To verify the radical criterion, if a morphism has zero quotient then $1-gf$ has identity quotient for every $g$; successive Gaussian block elimination chooses a scalar-unit pivot within each repeated class and gives an inverse, since its Schur complement retains identity quotient. Conversely a nonzero quotient component permits a matrix $g$ whose product has eigenvalue one, making $1-q(gf)$ singular. Thus this ideal is exactly the categorical radical and the quotient is semisimple with the stated simples. [given, F1, F3, algebra]

1.2 We need normalized character bar-invariance before discussing perverse summands. Induct on the Bruhat length of $x$. A reduced word for $x$ has bar-fixed character, the product of its bar-fixed simple generators by the locally proved recursion. Its decomposition is $B_x$ once and shifted lower-label summands by top-support classification. Perfect word duality and normalized self-duality pair the lower multiplicities in opposite shifts. By induction every lower normalized character is bar fixed, so subtracting their paired, bar-fixed contributions from the word character proves that $\operatorname{ch}(B_x)$ is bar fixed as well. Their leading terms are $H_x$ with coefficient one, so these normalized characters form a triangular Laurent-polynomial basis of the finite Hecke module, independently of the Kazhdan-Lusztig conjecture. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 On each object its radical is the Jacobson radical of its finite-dimensional endomorphism algebra by the invertibility criterion just proved. Its powers are nilpotent by the finite-algebra minimal-generator proof in the top-support classification supplier: a stabilized nonzero power would have a generating list shortened by solving against $1-a$ with $a$ radical. If $q(f)$ is invertible, lift an inverse $g$. Both $gf$ and $fg$ are $1$ plus a nilpotent radical element, and finite geometric series invert them; the resulting left and right inverses of $f$ coincide. Thus $q$ reflects isomorphisms and (1) holds. [step 1.1, F1, algebra]

2.2 Let $P$ be perverse. Its standard coefficients have no negative powers, because its character is a nonnegative integer combination of KL elements with lower coefficients in $v\mathbb Z[v]$. In a decomposition $P=\bigoplus B_y(d)$, each summand has nonnegative standard multiplicities; hence each summand also has no negative powers. Its top coefficient is $v^d$, giving $d\ge0$. The coefficients in the normalized-character basis are therefore polynomials $\sum_d m_{y,d}v^d$ with nonnegative powers. Both $\operatorname{ch}(P)$ and the basis elements are bar fixed by step 1.2, so each such polynomial is inversion invariant and therefore constant. Thus only shift zero occurs. Every resulting normalized summand has polynomial standard coefficients; its expansion in the KL basis has polynomial coefficients by descending triangular elimination. Bar-invariance forces these coefficients to be constant. Each constant is the constant term of a standard coefficient, since strict lower KL coefficients are divisible by $v$, and hence is nonnegative. Every summand is therefore perverse. A p-split object decomposes into shifts of perverse objects; applying this result to those pieces and uniqueness of Krull-Schmidt decompositions shows that each of its indecomposable shifts is a shift of a perverse indecomposable, and every summand remains p-split. This proves (3) without asserting that the character of a p-split object itself is bar fixed. [F1, F2, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 A differential with nonzero quotient has a nonzero matrix entry between copies of the same indecomposable class. That entry is outside its maximal ideal, hence is invertible. Gaussian elimination [F3] splits off a contractible two-term summand. Repeating decreases the finite total number of indecomposable terms and terminates with a minimal direct summand homotopy equivalent to the original complex. Between minimal complexes a homotopy equivalence becomes a degreewise isomorphism after $q$, since both differentials are zero there; reflection from step 2.1 makes it an isomorphism of complexes already before $q$. This proves existence and uniqueness in (2). [F1, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1]

3.2 For perverse $P,Q$, their standard characters have no negative powers, and the $\nabla$ character of a perverse object equals its $\Delta$ character: its decomposition in step 2.2 has only normalized self-dual unshifted summands, and right duality exchanges the two flag characters. The actual Hom formula thus gives a polynomial graded Hom rank with no negative powers. Since the polynomial ring has no negative degrees, every negative-degree map vanishes, giving $\operatorname{Hom}(P,Q(-i))=0$ for $i>0$. In shifted perverse indecomposables, $\operatorname{Hom}^0(P(k),Q(l))=\operatorname{Hom}^{l-k}(P,Q)$, so a nonzero component requires $l\ge k$. Thus a degree-zero morphism preserves each cut consisting of shifts $k\ge-j$; applying this to an isomorphism of decompositions and its inverse makes the cuts independent of the decomposition. This proves (4) and (5). [F1, F2, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 The bound classes are defined by existence of a homotopy-equivalent representative with p-split terms satisfying the relevant bounds. If such a representative exists, its minimal model is a termwise summand obtained by step 3.1; summands remain p-split by step 2.2 and inherit either cut bound by step 3.2. Conversely the minimal model itself is a representative. Hence either class can be tested on the minimal model. This does not assert that every arbitrary representative, after adding contractible terms, satisfies its bounds. [step 3.1, step 2.2, step 3.2]

5.1 For a triangle $F'\to F\to F''\to F'[1]$ whose outside objects satisfy a bound, choose their bounded p-split representatives. Represent $F$ by the cone of a map $F''[-1]\to F'$. Its degree-$i$ term is $F'^i\oplus F''^i$, since the cone shifts the first input once, undoing its $[-1]$. Both summands satisfy exactly the same degree-$i$ cut inequality; their direct sum does too. This works for either bound and proves extension closure. Together with step 4.1 it proves (6) and completes the lemma. [step 3.2, step 4.1] ∎
