items.title: Positive Rouquier complexes are Delta-split
items.statement:
Let $\underline x$ be a reduced expression for $x\in S_n$ and let $F_{\underline x}$ be the Rouquier complex $F_{s_1}\cdots F_{s_m}$ (or its minimal subcomplex). Then for every $y\in S_n$ there is an isomorphism in the homotopy category of graded bimodules
$$\Gamma_{\ge y}(F_{\underline x})/\Gamma_{>y}(F_{\underline x})\;\cong\;\begin{cases}\Delta_x,&y=x,\\0,&y\ne x,\end{cases}$$
where $\Delta_x=R_x(-\ell(x))$. Equivalently: the Bruhat support subquotient of a positive Rouquier complex is contractible except in the top layer $\Delta_x$; $F_{\underline x}$ is $\Delta$-split in the sense that each of its support subquotients is a direct sum of standard bimodules, and the top layer is a single $\Delta_x$. No positivity of characters and no assumption $\mathrm{S}$ is used; the statement is unconditional for every finite type-$A$ Coxeter group and the coordinate reflection realization.
items.strategy:
1.1 Induct on the word length. For the empty word $F_e=R$ has just $\Delta_e$; for one letter the exact rank-one sequence is $0\to R_s(-1)\to B_s\xrightarrow{\mu}R(1)\to0$. Its upper $s$ layer is $R_s(-1)=\Delta_s$, and its identity layer is the isomorphism $R(1)\to R(1)$, hence contractible. This starts the induction directly for positive complexes; no inverse generator is identified with a positive one. [base, given, F1]

1.2 Choose a Bruhat-compatible enumeration grouped into right-$s$ cosets, listing $y$ before $ys$ when $y<ys$. This exists by ordering the minimal representatives of the finite cosets in Bruhat order and refining each pair; the lifting property from reduced subwords ensures that different coset comparisons respect this order. Every union of complete initial or terminal cosets is right-$s$-stable. For such a set $A$, $\Gamma_A(MB_s)=\Gamma_A(M)B_s$: the cut and quotient have graph flags, whose free layers split on the right; after exact tensoring, their generic graph supports lie respectively in $A$ and its stable complement. The quotient remains right-free by its flag, so an $A$-supported element of it is generically zero and hence zero. This proves the cut identity and its analogous consecutive-coset quotient identity. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Write $x=zs$ with $\ell(x)=\ell(z)+1$. Every term of $F_z$ is supported on subexpressions of a reduced word for $z$, hence on labels at most $z$. In particular its $x$ layer is zero termwise, not merely contractible. Its paired layer on $\{z,x\}$ is therefore its single $z$ layer, homotopy equivalent as a full bimodule complex to $\Delta_z$ by induction. The cut identity of step 1.2 identifies the paired layer of $F_zF_s$ with the cone of the natural multiplication map from this paired layer tensored with $B_s$ to its shift $(1)$. A full bimodule homotopy equivalence commutes with this natural counit and induces a homotopy equivalence of the cones. Thus this paired layer is the rank-one graph complex $[R_z(-\ell(z))B_s\to R_z(-\ell(z)+1)]$. Its high $x$ layer is the kernel graph $R_x(-\ell(x))=\Delta_x$, and its low $z$ layer is an isomorphism onto $R_z(-\ell(z)+1)$ and contracts. The two single-layer functors of the paired layer are the original canonical single layers: the support cut and quotient flag, in the chosen enumeration, contain exactly those two labels, so their submodule and quotient are respectively its high and low graph layers. This proves the two required layers with the counit compatibility retained. [step 1.1, step 1.2, F1, F2, ih]

3.1 On any other pair, both single layers of $F_z$ contract by induction. Their paired sequence becomes termwise split after restriction to right $R^s$, by [F1]. Tensoring with $B_s$ yields a triangle with contractible outside terms, so its paired tensor layer contracts. Applying either single-layer functor preserves its homotopy and gives contractible single layers of $F_zB_s$. The same single layers of $F_z(1)$ contract already by induction. Since $F_zF_s$ is the cone of the natural multiplication map $F_zB_s\to F_z(1)$ with its standard shift, and an additive layer functor commutes with cones, both resulting single layers also contract. This treats every non-top pair without claiming that arbitrary complexes with zero Euler character contract. [step 1.2, step 2.1, F1, F2, ih]

4.1 The paired enumeration covers every graph; its single layers equal the canonical Bruhat layers by [F1]. Steps 2.1 and 3.1 prove the asserted homotopy isomorphism for the word complex. By [F3] every layer of a removed contractible summand remains contractible, so the same isomorphism holds for its minimal summand. This is exactly the stated $\Delta$-split property, obtained without any $S$ or Hodge assumption. [step 2.1, step 3.1, F1, F3, discharge-induction: step 3.1] ∎

items.title: Signature constancy in a Lefschetz family, the L-stable subspace lemma and the weak-Lefschetz substitute
items.statement:
(1) **Family lemma.** Let $L_t$, $t\in[a,b]$, be a continuous family of symmetric degree-two operators on $H$, each satisfying hL, and suppose $L_{t_0}$ satisfies HR with the standard sign for one $t_0\in[a,b]$. Then every $L_t$ satisfies HR with the standard sign; in the application the family is $L_\zeta$, $\zeta\ge0$, which is polynomial (hence continuous) in $\zeta$.

(2) **Weak-Lefschetz substitute.** Let $\varphi:V\to W(1)$ be a map of graded $R[L]$-modules such that (a) $\varphi$ is injective in degrees $\le-1$, (b) $V,W$ carry graded forms with $\langle\varphi(a),\varphi(b)\rangle_W=\langle a,Lb\rangle_V$, and (c) $W$ satisfies HR with the standard sign. Then $L^i:V^{-i}\to V^i$ is injective for all $i\ge0$, and if $\dim V^i=\dim V^{-i}$ for all $i$ then $L$ satisfies hL on $V$.

(3) **Sign bookkeeping.** If in (2) the lowest degree of $W$ is $-\ell$ and of $V$ is $-(\ell+1)$, then the Lefschetz form on $V^{-(\ell+1)}$ is $\pm$definite with the same sign as on $W^{-\ell}$, so if $V$ satisfies HR with the standard sign then $V$ has the standard sign if and only if $W$ does.

(4) **Degenerate shifted case.** Let the form on $H$ not be assumed non-degenerate and suppose $L^i:H^{-d-i}\to H^{-d+i}$ is an isomorphism for all $i\ge0$ with $d$ a positive integer. Then the Lefschetz form $(h,h')_L^{-i}=\langle h,L^ih'\rangle$ on $H^{-i}$ is identically zero for every $i\ge0$.

(5) **Stable-subspace lemma.** If $(H,L,\langle-,-\rangle)$ satisfies hL and HR and $V\subseteq H$ is an $L$-stable graded subspace with $\dim V^{-i}=\dim V^i$ for all $i$, then the restricted operator and form satisfy hL and HR on $V$ with the ambient degree-by-degree signs; the restricted form is non-degenerate, and its standard global sign agrees with the ambient standard sign if the lowest nonzero degrees agree.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct; continuous signature families and primitive-string bookkeeping.

1.1 **The family lemma (1).** Fix $i\ge0$ and consider the family of symmetric forms $(a,b)\mapsto\langle a,L_t^ib\rangle$ on the fixed space $H^{-i}$. For each $t$ it is non-degenerate, because hL makes $L_t^i:H^{-i}\to H^i$ an isomorphism and the ambient form pairs $H^i$ perfectly with $H^{-i}$; and it depends continuously on $t$ because $L_t$ does. At any parameter $t_*$, fix a real congruence diagonalizing its nonsingular matrix by [F1]. In this fixed basis all leading pivots at $t_*$ are nonzero. Symmetric elimination expresses successive pivots as continuous rational functions of the matrix entries near $t_*$; the denominators stay nonzero, and continuity of these finite sums, products and reciprocals follows by the elementary epsilon estimates for real arithmetic. By [F2], every pivot keeps its sign on a common neighborhood, so Sylvester inertia and hence signature are locally constant. A locally constant function on an interval is constant: otherwise the supremum of the initial interval on which its value agrees with the starting value contradicts local constancy at that supremum. Thus the signature is constant on $[a,b]$. At $t_0$ the primitive decomposition of $L_{t_0}$ is orthogonal for this form with definite primitive blocks, so the signature at every $t$ equals the $t_0$ signature. Moreover the primitive dimensions are the same for every $t$: $\dim P_{L_t}^{-i}=\dim H^{-i}-\dim H^{-i-2}$ for all $t$, by the string decomposition of [F1] applied to each $L_t$. Descending induction on $i$ from the top degree in the signature formula of [F1] now shows that the primitive Lefschetz forms of $L_t$ have the $t_0$-signs for every $t$: at the top nonzero degree the signature of $H^{-i}$ is the signature of the primitive form, and inductively subtract the contributions of the already-determined higher primitive spaces, whose dimensions do not depend on $t$. Orthogonality and hL make the primitive forms non-degenerate, and the signature subtraction forces their signatures to be the prescribed signs times their dimensions. Sylvester inertia then gives the standard-sign definiteness for every $t$. In the application $L_\zeta=L_0+\zeta M$ with $M$ the middle-position operator is polynomial in $\zeta$, hence continuous on $[0,\infty)$ and on every compact subinterval. This proves (1). [given, F1, F2]

2.1 **The weak-Lefschetz substitute, injectivity (2).** For $i=0$ the map $L^0$ is the identity. Let $i\ge1$ and $0\ne a\in V^{-i}$; then $-i\le-1$, so $\varphi(a)\ne0$ by (a). If $L^i\varphi(a)\ne0$, then $L^i a\ne0$ because $L^i\varphi(a)=\varphi(L^i a)$ (the map is $R[L]$-linear). Otherwise $L^i\varphi(a)=0$, so $\varphi(a)$ is a nonzero primitive vector in $W^{-i+1}$; the HR relations of $W$ give that the Lefschetz value $(\varphi(a),\varphi(a))_L^{-i+1}=\langle\varphi(a),L^{i-1}\varphi(a)\rangle_W$ is definite nonzero. By (b) this equals $\langle a,L^ia\rangle_V$; in particular $L^ia\ne0$. Hence $L^i$ is injective in both cases. If moreover $\dim V^{-i}=\dim V^i$ for all $i$, injectivity plus equality of finite dimensions makes each $L^i:V^{-i}\to V^i$ an isomorphism, which is hL on $V$. This proves (2). [step 1.1, given, F1]

3.1 **Sign bookkeeping (3).** In the situation of step 2.1 with $i=\ell+1$, one has $-i+1=-\ell$, the lowest degree of $W$, and the image of $V^{-(\ell+1)}$ lies in $W^{-\ell}$, whose $(\ell+1)$-st power under $L$ is zero because $W^{\ell+2}=0$. Thus the primitive branch of step 2.1 applies to every such image and shows that the Lefschetz form on $V^{-(\ell+1)}$ is definite with the sign of the primitive form of $W$ in degree $-\ell$, which is the sign prescribed by the standard-sign HR of $W$; the global factor of the HR statement of $V$, if any, is thereby fixed, and $V$ has the standard sign exactly when $W$ does. This proves (3). [step 2.1, F1]

4.1 **The degenerate shifted case (4).** Put $Q_L^{-d-i}:=\ker(L^{i+1}|_{H^{-d-i}})\subseteq H^{-d-i}$ for $i\ge0$, and $Q^{-d-i}_L:=0$ for $i<0$. The hypothesis that $L^i:H^{-d-i}\to H^{-d+i}$ is an isomorphism for all $i\ge0$ gives the shifted primitive decomposition $H^m=\bigoplus_{j\ge0}L^jQ_L^{m-2j}$ by the same string argument as the primitive decomposition of [F1], with the centering shifted by $d$. Fix $m\le0$, $x\in Q^{m-2j}_L$, $y\in Q^{m-2k}_L$ with $j\ge k\ge0$; then $(L^jx,L^ky)_L^m=\langle x,L^{j+k-m}y\rangle$. Now $y\in Q^{m-2k}_L=\ker(L^{i+1})$ with $-d-i=m-2k$, i.e. $i=2k-m-d$, so $y$ is killed by $L^{2k-m-d+1}$; and $j+k-m\ge 2k-m-d+1$ because $j\ge k\ge k-d+1$ as $d>0$. Hence the pairing vanishes for arbitrary primitive vectors and arbitrary blocks, so the Lefschetz form on $H^m$ is identically zero. This proves (4). [step 3.1, given, F1, algebra]

5.1 **The stable-subspace lemma (5).** Let $V\subseteq H$ be $L$-stable with symmetric dimensions. Since $L^i:H^{-i}\to H^i$ is injective, its restriction to $V^{-i}$ is injective, and the dimension equality makes it an isomorphism onto $V^i$; so $V$ satisfies hL. The primitive subspace of $V$ is $P_V^{-i}=V^{-i}\cap P_L^{-i}$, because the kernel of $L^{i+1}$ on $V^{-i}$ is the intersection of $V^{-i}$ with the kernel on $H^{-i}$; the restricted Lefschetz form on $P_V^{-i}$ is the restriction of the ambient definite primitive form, hence definite with the ambient sign $(-1)^{(d-i)/2}$. By the primitive decomposition applied inside $V$ (step 2.1 of [[lem-hard-lefschetz-implies-primitive-decomposition]] gives it from hL on $V$), the restricted form on $V$ is an orthogonal sum of definite blocks, hence non-degenerate, and its signs are the ambient signs; if the lowest nonzero degree of $V$ is $-d$, the ambient standard sign is also the standard sign of $V$. This proves (5) and completes the lemma; no choice principle is used. [step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, F1, F2] ∎

items.title: The local intersection form on Hom(B_y, B_x B_s)
items.statement:
**The setting.** Fix $x\in S_n$, a simple reflection $s$ with $xs>x$, and
$y<xs$ in the Bruhat order; assume $\mathrm{S}(z)$ for all $z<xs$. Choose
reduced-word embeddings $B_y^R\subseteq\!\!\bigoplus\mathrm{BS}(\underline y)$
and $B_x^R\subseteq\!\!\bigoplus\mathrm{BS}(\underline x)$, and equip $B_y^R$,
$B_x^R$ with the positively normalized non-degenerate invariant forms obtained
by restriction, so that the bottom Lefschetz values are $+1$; equip
$M:=B_x^RB_s^R$ with the induced invariant form of
[[def-invariant-intersection-form-on-a-bott-samelson-bimodule]]. Under
$\mathrm{S}(y)$ and $\mathrm{S}(x)$ these forms exist and are unique up to
positive scalars, and the choices enter only through positive factors
([[lem-invariant-forms-on-soergel-bimodules-are-unique-up-to-scalar-and-nondegenerate]]).

**The local intersection form.** Let
$$E_y:=\operatorname{Hom}^0(B_y^R,M)$$
be the finite-dimensional real space of degree-zero bimodule maps. For
$f,g\in E_y$ define the **local intersection form**
$$(f,g)^{x,s}_y:=g^*\circ f\ \in\ \operatorname{End}^0(B_y^R)=\mathbb R,$$
where $g^*:M\to B_y^R$ is the **adjoint** of $g$ with respect to the two
non-degenerate forms, uniquely characterized by
$\langle g(b),m\rangle_M=\langle b,g^*(m)\rangle_{B_y}$ for all $b\in B_y^R$,
$m\in M$; adjunction is the standard transpose operation of
[[def-transpose-of-a-linear-map]] under the identifications
$B_y^R\to (B_y^R)^*$ and $M\to M^*$ induced by the forms
([[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]]). The adjoint construction
identifies $\operatorname{Hom}^0(B_y^R,M)$ with
$\operatorname{Hom}^0(M,B_y^R)$.

**Basic properties.** The form $(-,-)^{x,s}_y$ is symmetric: the adjoint of
$g^*f$ is $f^*g$, and a scalar endomorphism of $B_y^R$ is self-adjoint for its
invariant form. It is $\mathbb R$-bilinear, and it changes only by a positive
scalar when the chosen normalized forms or reduced-word embeddings are varied:
scaling the form on $M$ by $a>0$ and the form on $B_y^R$ by $b>0$ scales
$(-,-)^{x,s}_y$ by $a/b$, and the invariant-form uniqueness lemma shows that any
two choices compare by positive scalars. Define
$$\mathrm{S}^\pm(y,x,s)$$
to mean that $(-,-)^{x,s}_y$ is definite of sign
$(-1)^{(\ell(x)+1-\ell(y))/2}$, respectively its negative, with the parity
convention of
[[def-primitive-subspaces-hard-lefschetz-and-hodge-riemann-signs]]: when the
numerator is odd the corresponding primitive space is zero and the sign
condition is not used.

**Status.** The definition uses degree-zero Hom throughout; no statement
identifies the rank of the full graded Hom module with a Kazhdan-Lusztig
multiplication coefficient. The dimension of $E_y$ in terms of the
multiplication formula, and the equivalence of non-degeneracy of these forms
with the actual summand multiplicities of $M$, are proved in the detection
theorem later on this page; they are not part of this definition.
items.strategy: The nondegenerate graded invariant forms identify each bimodule with its dual, so adjoints are well-defined degree-zero bimodule maps. Under S(y), End^0(B_y)=R, giving the scalar-valued composition. The adjoint of g* f is f* g, and a scalar endomorphism is self-adjoint, so the form is symmetric. Scaling the M-form by a positive scalar a and the B_y-form by a positive scalar b scales this form by a/b. The invariant-form uniqueness lemma ensures these comparisons are positive for all chosen reduced-word embeddings. The definition uses degree-zero Hom throughout; its quantitative detection properties have a separate proved supplier.

items.title: Tensoring a direct sum of Hodge-Riemann bimodules with B_s preserves the signs
items.statement: Fix $\zeta\ge0$ and a self-dual Soergel bimodule $B=\bigoplus_zB_z^{R,m_z}$ such that $m_z\ne0$ implies $\mathrm{S}(z)$ and $\mathrm{HR}(z,s)_\zeta$; if $\zeta=0$ assume in addition that $m_z=0$ whenever $zs<z$. Assume $B$ is even or odd, carries an invariant non-degenerate form and satisfies HR with the standard sign with respect to left multiplication by $\rho$. Then $BB_s$ satisfies HR with the standard sign with respect to $L_\zeta$ and the induced form. More precisely, if the lowest degree of $B$ is $-d$, then the restriction of its form to a $B_z$ summand is $(-1)^{(d-\ell(z))/2}$ times a positive multiple of the normalized form on $B_z$. Tensoring gives the primitive sign $(-1)^{(d+1-i)/2}$ on degree $-i$ of $BB_s$, whose lowest degree is $-d-1$.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct; orthogonal isotypic decomposition and sign bookkeeping over the tensor factors.

1.1 **Unshifted orthogonal blocks and their scalars.** By [F1] the given unshifted decomposition of $B$ has orthogonal isotypic components, with the normalized perfect $B_z$ form tensored with a nonsingular real symmetric multiplicity matrix. Orthogonally diagonalize these finite matrices to obtain orthogonal unshifted copies $B_z$ with form $c_\alpha\langle-,-\rangle_z$, where $c_\alpha\ne0$. In each copy its bottom vector has degree $-\ell(z)$ and is primitive, since $\rho^{\ell(z)+1}$ vanishes by the degree bounds. Its normalized Lefschetz value is positive by [F1]. Ambient HR on $B$ says the value on this primitive vector has sign $(-1)^{(d-\ell(z))/2}$. Hence $c_\alpha$ has exactly that sign. This proves the claimed scalar comparison for every copy, including components which do not attain the bottom degree of $B$. No grading shifts are introduced. [given, F1, F3]

1.2 **Tensoring preserves the orthogonal decomposition and stability.** Tensoring the chosen decomposition of $B$ with $B_s$ gives an orthogonal decomposition $BB_s=\bigoplus_\alpha B_{z_\alpha}^{R}B_s$ for the induced form, because the induced form on a direct sum is the orthogonal sum of the induced forms and the isotypic components remain mutually orthogonal. The deformed operator $L_\zeta$ is built from left multiplication by $\rho$ on the first factor and middle multiplication on the tensor position, so it preserves each block $B_z^RB_s$: the projections onto the blocks are bimodule maps commuting with left multiplication on the first factor, and middle multiplication by $\rho$ acts inside the balanced tensor position and commutes with the outer actions; hence the restriction of $L_\zeta$ to each block is the operator of the same name on that block. [given, F1, F2]

2.1 **Primitive signs on the blocks.** On each block $B_z^RB_s$ satisfying $\mathrm{HR}(z,s)_\zeta$, the primitive space in degree $-i$ is definite with sign $(-1)^{(\ell(z)+1-i)/2}$ by [F2], relative to the induced form normalized with bottom value $+1$; the actual restricted form differs from that normalization by the scalar of step 1.1, which is the sign $(-1)^{(d-\ell(z))/2}$ times a positive number, and a positive scalar changes no definiteness sign. The product of the two signs is $(-1)^{(d-\ell(z)+\ell(z)+1-i)/2}=(-1)^{(d+1-i)/2}$, independent of $z$; hence each block's primitive signs are the common standard signs of $BB_s$, whose lowest degree is $-d-1$: the bottom of each block is $-\ell(z)-1$, and the largest occurring $\ell(z)$ equals $d$ in the unshifted sum. [step 1.1, step 1.2, F2, algebra]

3.1 **The descent summands at $\zeta=0$ and conclusion.** If $\zeta=0$ the hypothesis excludes summands with $zs<z$, so every block $B_z^RB_s$ is an ascent block or has $zs>z$; no HR statement for a shifted descent block is used. By [F3] the orthogonal sum of the blocks satisfies HR with the common standard signs of step 2.1, and the lowest-degree sign is positive by the normalization of the bottom: the total bottom is $\bigoplus_{z\text{ at bottom}}B_z^{-\ell(z)}B_s^{-1}$, and each block contributes a positive multiple of its bottom primitive form, so the assembled form is positive there. Hence $BB_s$ satisfies HR with the standard sign with respect to $L_\zeta$ and the induced form, and the displayed sign $(-1)^{(d+1-i)/2}$ is exactly the standard sign of the tensor product; this completes the proof. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, F1, F3] ∎

items.title: Right-descent Soergel bimodules descend to simple invariants under the character hypothesis
items.statement:
Let $M=B_x^R$ over $S$ and let $s$ be a right descent, $xs<x$. Assume $\mathrm{S}(x)$. Then there is a graded $(S,S^s)$-bimodule $N$ and an isomorphism $M\cong N\otimes_{S^s}S$. Consequently $MB_s=M(1)\oplus M(-1)$; choosing the decomposition $S=S^s\oplus(\alpha_s/2)S^s$ in the middle tensor factor, the reduced operator $L_\zeta$ has, with respect to the resulting identification $MB_s=M(1)\oplus M(-1)$, the matrix
$$L_\zeta=\begin{pmatrix}\rho\cdot(-)&0\\ \zeta\rho(\alpha_s^\vee)&\rho\cdot(-)\end{pmatrix},$$
where the scalar off-diagonal entry is a degree-two map $M(1)\to M(-1)$. The construction requires no singular-category classification or character conjecture beyond $\mathrm{S}(x)$. If $\mathrm{hL}(x)$ also holds and $\zeta>0$, this matrix satisfies centered hard Lefschetz; at $\zeta=0$ it fails centered hard Lefschetz.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** construct the descent isomorphism from a split counit, then compute the matrix and the Lefschetz strings.

1.1 **A genuine bimodule section.** Put $U=M\otimes_{S^s}S$, so $MB_s=U(1)$. The actual bimodule decomposition of [F1] gives $U\cong M\oplus M(-2)$. The multiplication counit $c:U\to M$, $c(b\otimes r)=br$, is an $S$-bimodule map. The bottom degree of $U$ is the single line $M^{-\ell(x)}\otimes1$, on which $c$ is nonzero. Only the unshifted summand $M$ in this decomposition has that degree, so $c$ restricts to a nonzero degree-zero endomorphism of that summand. By [F1] it is a nonzero scalar, hence invertible. Compose its inverse with the actual bimodule inclusion to obtain a degree-zero bimodule section $\sigma:M\to U$. On the bottom line $\sigma(b)=b\otimes1$, because $c\sigma=1$ and that line in $U$ is one dimensional. [given, F1, F2]

2.1 **The twisted counit.** Define $c_s:U\to M_s$ by $c_s(b\otimes r)=b\,s(r)$. It is balanced over $S^s$, left $S$-linear and right-$s$-semilinear. Since the section $\sigma$ in step 1.1 is genuinely right-$S$-linear, $t=c_s\sigma:M\to M$ is degree zero, left $S$-linear and right-$s$-semilinear. It is the identity on the bottom line by step 1.1. This argument uses the actual bimodule summand, rather than the generally non-right-linear map $b\mapsto b\otimes1$. [step 1.1, F1, F2]

3.1 **The involution property of $t$.** Since $t$ is right-$s$-semilinear and degree zero, $t^2$ is an ordinary degree-zero $S$-bimodule endomorphism of $M$, hence a scalar by $\operatorname{End}^0(M)=\mathbb R$; its scalar is $1$ because $t^2$ acts as the identity on the one-dimensional bottom degree by step 2.1. Hence $t^2=\mathrm{id}_M$. [step 2.1, F1]

4.1 **The descent isomorphism.** For $u\in U$ one has $c_s(u)-c(u)\in M\alpha_s$, because $s(r)-r\in\alpha_s S$ for every $r\in S$; consequently $t(m)-m\in M\alpha_s$ for every $m\in M$. Define $N:=\{m\in M: t(m)=m\}$. Every $m$ splits as $m=\tfrac12(m+t(m))+\tfrac12(m-t(m))$ into an invariant and an anti-invariant part, and an anti-invariant $m$ (that is, $t(m)=-m$) lies in $M\alpha_s$, say $m=n\alpha_s$; since right multiplication by $\alpha_s$ is injective by [F2] and $t(m)=-m$ with $s(\alpha_s)=-\alpha_s$ gives $t(n\alpha_s)=t(n)s(\alpha_s)=-t(n)\alpha_s$ and hence $t(n)=n$, we get $n\in N$ and the anti-invariant part of $m$ is $N\alpha_s$. Therefore $M=N\oplus N\alpha_s$ as $(S,S^s)$-bimodules, and the multiplication map induces an isomorphism $N\otimes_{S^s}S\to M$; this proves the descent isomorphism. [step 2.1, step 3.1, F1, F2]

5.1 **The matrix of $L_\zeta$.** Use the proved descent $M=N\otimes_{S^s}S$ to write $MB_s=N\otimes_{S^s}S\otimes_{S^s}S(1)$. Splitting the middle factor by $S=S^s\oplus(\alpha_s/2)S^s$ gives the bimodule isomorphism $MB_s\cong M(1)\oplus M(-1)$, with structure maps $\iota_1,\iota_2,\pi_1,\pi_2$ of [F2] satisfying $\pi_a\iota_b=\delta_{ab}$. In this basis, middle multiplication by $\rho$ has entries $\pi_1(\rho)$, $\pi_1(\alpha_s\rho)/2$, $\rho(\alpha_s^\vee)$ and $\partial_s(\alpha_s\rho)/2$, and the operators of multiplication by $\rho$ on the two outer factors contribute the same diagonal $\rho\cdot(-)$ on $M(1)$ and $M(-1)$. All entries except the off-diagonal $\rho(\alpha_s^\vee)$ have positive polynomial degree in $\rho$ and vanish after the right reduction; the off-diagonal entry has the constant term $\rho(\alpha_s^\vee)$ and contributes the degree-two map $\zeta\rho(\alpha_s^\vee):M(1)\to M(-1)$; hence, after reduction, $L_\zeta$ is the displayed matrix. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 4.1, F2, algebra]

6.1 **Hard Lefschetz for $\zeta>0$.** Assume $\mathrm{hL}(x)$, so the reduced module $\overline M$ is a direct sum of centered $\rho$-strings $u_0,\ldots,u_m$ with $\deg u_j=-m+2j$ and $\rho u_j=u_{j+1}$; on each string, left multiplication by $\rho$ is the standard nilpotent Jordan block. In the two-dimensional middle factor with basis $v_-,v_+$ of degrees $-1,+1$ and $e(v_-)=\zeta\rho(\alpha_s^\vee)v_+$, $e(v_+)=0$, the operator $e=L_\zeta$ on the string tensor $\bigoplus_j u_j\otimes\{v_-,v_+\}$ acts by $e^k(u_jv_-)=u_{j+k}v_-+k\,u_{j+k-1}v_+$ and $e^k(u_jv_+)=u_{j+k}v_+$ (indices out of range zero), after normalizing the nonzero scalar $\zeta\rho(\alpha_s^\vee)$ to $1$ by rescaling $v_+$; for $0\le k\le m-1$ of the compatible parity $k\equiv m+1\pmod2$, in centered degree $-k$ the source basis $u_{(m+1-k)/2}v_-,\,u_{(m-1-k)/2}v_+$ and the corresponding target basis exhibit $e^k$ as a matrix with diagonal entries $1$ and $1$, lower-left entry $k$, and upper-right entry $0$, which is invertible; at $k=m+1$ the map sends $u_0v_-$ to $(m+1)u_mv_+$, nonzero by the normalization $\zeta\rho(\alpha_s^\vee)>0$. The operator on each string is thus an isomorphism in every centered degree, and $L_\zeta$ on the direct sum of strings satisfies hL. Positivity of $\zeta\rho(\alpha_s^\vee)$ uses $\zeta>0$ and strict dominance of $\rho$. [step 5.1, F1, algebra]

7.1 **Failure at $\zeta=0$ and conclusion.** At $\zeta=0$ the matrix of step 5.1 is diagonal with respect to the decomposition $MB_s=M(1)\oplus M(-1)$. The bottom class $b\in\overline M^{-\ell(x)}$ sits in the first summand in degree $-\ell(x)-1$ and satisfies $\rho^{\ell(x)+1}b=0$ because $\overline M^{\ell(x)+2}=0$; the opposite class in $M(-1)$ of degree $\ell(x)+1$ is nonzero by self-duality and dimension symmetry. Hence $\rho^{\ell(x)+1}$ is not injective on $\overline{MB_s}$ in the centered grading and centered hL fails at $\zeta=0$, even though the two individual shifted copies of $\overline M$ have their own strings centered at $\pm1$. Steps 1.1-5.1 prove the descent isomorphism and the matrix, step 6.1 the positive-parameter hard Lefschetz, and this step the failure at zero; no singular-category classification or character conjecture beyond $\mathrm{S}(x)$ is used. [step 5.1, step 6.1, F1, F3] ∎

items.title: Minimal positive Rouquier complexes are linear under the lower Soergel induction
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** induction on the length; the perverse lower bound is propagated through the stupid filtration, the upper bound and the labels through the shift-propagation lemma, and the coefficients through inversion of the unitriangular Kazhdan-Lusztig transition matrix.

1.1 **Base of the induction.** [base] For $x=e$ the Rouquier complex is the unit $S$ concentrated in cohomological degree $0$, so $^0F_e=S=B_e$, there is no term of index $i\ge1$, both perverse bounds hold trivially, and the only nonzero inverse coefficient is $g_{e,e}=1$; for $x=s_i$ the complex $F_{s_i}=[B_{s_i}^R\to S(1)]$ has $^0F_{s_i}=B_{s_i}$ and $^1F_{s_i}=S(1)=B_e^R(1)$ and no other term, so $m_{e,1}=1$ with $\ell(s_i)-\ell(e)=1\equiv1\pmod2$, $B_{s_i}$ is perverse by $\mathrm S(s_i)$ and $S(1)$ is the shift of the perverse unit, so $F_{s_i}\in pK^b_{\ge0}\cap pK^b_{\le0}$ and $g_{s_i,s_i}=1$, $g_{e,s_i}=-v$. [given, F1, F3, F5]

2.1 **Induction hypothesis and the last letter.** [ih] Fix $x\ne e$, write $\underline x=s_1\cdots s_m$ with $m\ge1$ and put $y=s_1\cdots s_{m-1}$, $s=s_m$, so that $x=ys$ with $\ell(x)=\ell(y)+1$; the hypothesis $\mathrm S(\le x)$ contains $\mathrm S(\le y)$, and we assume the three assertions of the statement for $y$: $^0F_y=B_y$, $^iF_y=\bigoplus_{z<y}B_z(i)^{m^y_{z,i}}$ for $i\ge1$, and $F_y\in pK^b_{\ge0}\cap pK^b_{\le0}$. By [F1], $F_x\cong F_yF_s$ in $K^b$. [given, step 1.1, F1]

3.1 **Descent contraction.** Let $z$ and a simple reflection $s$ satisfy $zs<z$ and $\mathrm S(z)$; then $B_zF_s\cong B_z(-1)$ in $K^b$. Indeed, by [F2] the two-term complex $B_zF_s$ has terms $B_zB_s=B_z(1)\oplus B_z(-1)$ in degree $0$ and $B_z(1)$ in degree $1$, with differential $d=(\delta,\eta)$ where $\delta\in\operatorname{End}^0(B_z(1))=\operatorname{End}^0(B_z)=\mathbb R$ by [F2] and [F6]. If $\delta=0$ then $B_zF_s$ is the direct sum of the two nonzero complexes $[B_z(1)\to0]$ and $[B_z(-1)\xrightarrow{\ \eta\ }B_z(1)]$, contradicting the indecomposability of $B_zF_s$, which is the image of the indecomposable $B_z$ under the equivalence $-\otimes F_s$; hence $\delta\ne0$ is an isomorphism, homological Gaussian elimination cancels the contractible two-term complex $B_z(1)\cong B_z(1)$, and the remainder is $B_z(-1)$ concentrated in degree $0$. [step 2.1, F1, F2, F6]

3.2 **Top support and the Euler character.** Every positive-degree term of the word complex omits at least one letter, so no such term has the $x$ graph by [F3]. The degree-zero term is its reduced word, whose top summand is exactly $B_x$ unshifted and once. Gaussian minimalization cannot remove it, since no target term has its label. Thus in the minimal complex $m^0_{x,0}=1$ and every other $m^i_{x,k}$ is zero, by actual support rather than alternating cancellation. Character additivity makes its Euler character unchanged by removing a contractible pair. The generator recursion and shift rule in [F3] give $\operatorname{ch}(F_zF_s)=\operatorname{ch}(F_z)(\underline H_s-v)$ degree by degree. Iterating along the reduced word therefore gives Euler character $H_x$. Under the stated $S(\le x)$, expanding each actual summand character in the KL basis yields $\sum_{i,k}(-1)^im^i_{w,k}v^k=g_{w,x}$. This equality is used only for the Euler coefficients, after the support proof of the top multiplicity. [step 2.1, F1, F3, F4]

4.1 **Ascent perverse bound.** Let $z\le y$ and a simple reflection $s$ satisfy $zs>z$; then $B_zF_s\in pK^b_{\ge0}$. Indeed, $\mathrm S(u)$ holds for every $u<zs$, because $u<zs\le x$ implies $u<x$; so [F2] gives the unshifted decomposition $B_zB_s=B_{zs}\oplus\bigoplus_{u<zs}B_u^{a_u}$, whose summands are perverse by $\mathrm S(zs)$ and $\mathrm S(u)$, while the second term $B_z(1)$ of $B_zF_s=[B_zB_s\to B_z(1)]$ is the internal shift of the perverse $B_z$ sitting in cohomological degree $1$; thus the chosen representative has p-split terms and satisfies $\tau_{<0}(B_zB_s)=0$ and $\tau_{<-1}(B_z(1))=0$, which is membership in $pK^b_{\ge0}$ by [F5]. [step 3.1, F2, F5]

4.2 **Shift propagation.** Assume $\mathrm S(\le x)$ and let $F_x$ be minimal. If $^iF_x$ contains a summand $B_z(j)$ with $z<x$, then $^{i-1}F_x$ contains a summand $B_{z'}(j')$ with $z'>z$ and $j'<j$. First, components of the differential into summands of shift $k<j$ vanish: a degree-zero map $B_z(j)\to B_u(k)$ is an element of $\operatorname{Hom}^{k-j}(B_z,B_u)$, which is zero for $k<j$ since the graded Hom space has no negative-degree part by [F6]; components with $k=j$ are zero for $u\ne z$ by [F6] and are scalars for $u=z$, and a nonzero scalar component would make $B_z(j)$ a contractible summand of the minimal complex, so all such components vanish as well; hence $d(B_z(j))$ lies in the sum of the summands of $^{i+1}F_x$ with shift $k>j$. Second, if a summand $B_u(k)$ of $^{i-1}F_x$ maps nontrivially to $B_z(j)$, then $k<j$: a degree-zero map $B_u(k)\to B_z(j)$ lies in $\operatorname{Hom}^{j-k}(B_u,B_z)$, which vanishes for $j<k$, and for $j=k$ it vanishes for $u\ne z$ and is a scalar for $u=z$, the nonzero case again being excluded by minimality. Third, apply the support cutoff $\Gamma_{\ge z/>z}$ and reduce its free graph modules modulo $R_+$. Since $z<x$, its complex is contractible by [F5], hence this reduced finite-dimensional complex is exact. The chosen top layer $\Delta_z(j)$ of $B_z(j)$ is a nonzero homogeneous basis vector. Every outgoing target has shift $k>j$, and its $z$ layer has shift $k+d$ with $d\ge0$ by KL triangularity. A map from the chosen generator into it consequently has positive-degree coefficient, so vanishes after reduction. The chosen vector is a cycle and must therefore be an incoming boundary. Some incoming component has a nonzero constant coefficient onto it, so some $B_{z'}(j')$ in degree $i-1$ has a $z$ layer with $j'+d=j$. The underlying differential component is nonzero, and the preceding Hom estimate gives $j'<j$. Since $d=0$ for label $z$ itself, this requires $z'>z$. This proves shift propagation without using an Euler identity to recover multiplicities. [step 3.2, F2, F4, F5, F6]

5.1 **The perverse lower bound for $F_x$.** Use the stupid filtration $w_{\ge k}F_y$ of the minimal complex $F_y$, with distinguished triangles $w_{\ge k+1}F_y\to w_{\ge k}F_y\to{}^kF_y[-k]\to$ and $w_{\ge\ell(y)+1}F_y=0$; tensoring with the invertible $F_s$ preserves distinguished triangles. We prove $(w_{\ge k}F_y)F_s\in pK^b_{\ge0}$ by descending induction on $k$: for $k=\ell(y)+1$ the object is $0$; assume it for $k+1$. By [ih] and step 2.1, $^kF_y$ is a direct sum of summands $B_z(k)$ with $z\le y$ (with $z=y$ only for $k=0$), so $(^kF_y)F_s[-k]$ is a direct sum of copies of $(B_zF_s)(k)[-k]$. If $zs>z$ then $B_zF_s\in pK^b_{\ge0}$ by step 4.1, and its internal shift $(k)$ and homological shift $[-k]$ place every summand $B_u(\ell)$ occurring in cohomological degree $i$ into degree $i+k$ with internal shift $\ell+k\le i+k$, so $(B_zF_s)(k)[-k]\in pK^b_{\ge0}$; if $zs<z$  then step 3.1 gives $B_zF_s\cong B_z(-1)$, so $(B_zF_s)(k)[-k]\cong B_z(k-1)[-k]$, a perverse object with internal shift $k-1$ in cohomological degree $k$, again in $pK^b_{\ge0}$. Extension closure of $pK^b_{\ge0}$ in the tensored triangles gives $(w_{\ge k}F_y)F_s\in pK^b_{\ge0}$, and at $k=0$ we obtain $F_yF_s\in pK^b_{\ge0}$; by step 2.1 this is $F_x\in pK^b_{\ge0}$. [step 4.1, step 2.1, F1, F5, ih]

6.1 **The top term and the perverse upper bound.** If $^0F_x$ contained a summand $B_z(j)$ with $z<x$, then step 4.2 with $i=0$ would produce a summand of $^{-1}F_x=0$, which is impossible; hence every summand of $^0F_x$ has label $x$, and by step 3.2 ($m^0_{x,0}=1$ and $m^0_{x,k}=0$ for $k\ne0$) we get $^0F_x=B_x$, which proves (1). Now suppose $i\ge1$ and $^iF_x$ has a summand $B_z(k)$ with $k<i$; if $z=x$ this contradicts $m^i_{x,k}=0$ from step 3.2, so $z<x$, and step 4.2 produces a summand $B_{z'}(k')$ of $^{i-1}F_x$ with $k'<k<i$. This summand is again of the forbidden type: if $z'=x$ then $m^{i-1}_{x,k'}=0$ whenever $i-1\ge1$, while for $i-1=0$ it contradicts $^0F_x=B_x$ because $k'<0$; otherwise $z'<x$ and step 4.2 applies again. Iterating this descent in the homological degree we reach a summand of $^0F_x$ with negative internal shift, contradicting $^0F_x=B_x$. Hence every summand of $^iF_x$ has internal shift $\ge i$ for $i\ge1$, which together with $F_x\in pK^b_{\ge0}$ from step 5.1 gives $F_x\in pK^b_{\le0}$; since for $i\ge1$ the label $x$ does not occur by step 3.2, we obtain $^iF_x=\bigoplus_{z<x}B_z(i)^{m_{z,i}}$ with $m_{z,i}:=m^i_{z,i}$, which is (2). [step 4.2, step 5.1, F5]

7.1 **Inversion of the Kazhdan-Lusztig transition matrix.** Let the two bases be related by $\underline H_w=\sum_{y\le w}h_{y,w}H_y$ and $H_w=\sum_{y\le w}g_{y,w}\underline H_y$ as in [F4]; substituting the first expansion into the second gives $\sum_{y\le z\le w}h_{y,z}g_{z,w}=\delta_{y,w}$. Hence $g_{w,w}=1$ and, for $y<w$, $g_{y,w}=-\sum_{y<z\le w}h_{y,z}g_{z,w}$. We prove $g_{y,w}\in v^{\ell(w)-\ell(y)}\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$ by descending induction on $\ell(w)-\ell(y)$: for $y=w$ this is $1\in v^0\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$, and for $y<w$ each $h_{y,z}$ lies in $v^{\ell(z)-\ell(y)}\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$ by [F4] and each $g_{z,w}$ with $y<z\le w$ lies in $v^{\ell(w)-\ell(z)}\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$ by the hypothesis of the induction, so each product lies in $v^{\ell(w)-\ell(y)}\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$ and the finite sum does too. [step 6.1, F4, algebra]

8.1 **Parity and positivity of the inverse coefficients.** By step 3.2 and step 6.1 the multiplicities appearing in $g_{z,x}=\sum_i(-1)^im_{z,i}v^i$ are exactly the multiplicities of the linear complex $F_x$, and by step 7.1 we have $g_{z,x}\in v^{\ell(x)-\ell(z)}\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$; therefore the coefficient $(-1)^im_{z,i}$ of $v^i$ can be nonzero only when $i\equiv\ell(x)-\ell(z)\pmod2$, which is the parity clause of (3). For such $i$ the sign $(-1)^{\ell(x)-\ell(z)+i}$ equals $+1$, so $(-1)^{\ell(x)-\ell(z)}g_{z,x}=\sum_i(-1)^{\ell(x)-\ell(z)+i}m_{z,i}v^i\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}[v^{\pm1}]$, and the coefficients are the nonnegative multiplicities $m_{z,i}$. This proves (3) and, with (1) and (2), completes the induction. [step 7.1, step 3.2, discharge-induction: step 2.1] ∎

items.title: Undeformed Lefschetz and Hodge-Riemann restrict to the next Soergel summand
items.statement:
Let $xs>x$. The normalized indecomposable $B_{xs}^R$ occurs as a bimodule summand of $B_x^RB_s^R$.

(a) If $\mathrm{hL}(x,s)_0$ holds, then $\mathrm{hL}(xs)$ holds.

(b) If $\mathrm{S}(<xs)$ and $\mathrm{hL}(y)$ for every $y<xs$ hold, then $\mathrm{hL}(x,s)_0$ is equivalent to $\mathrm{hL}(xs)$.

(c) If $\mathrm{HRbar}(x,s)_0$ holds, then the restriction to the chosen $B_{xs}^R$ summand satisfies the Hodge-Riemann relations for its induced form; once $\mathrm{S}(xs)$ has been established, positive comparison of invariant forms gives $\mathrm{HR}(xs)$ and $\mathrm{HRbar}(xs)$ with the standard sign.

(d) More generally an $L_0$-stable graded subspace with symmetric Betti numbers inherits HR with the ambient signs, and an $L_0$-stable graded direct summand inherits hL. These conclusions apply to a positive deformation only if the chosen subspace, and for the direct-sum argument its complement, are preserved by that operator; they make no identification of the restricted positive operator with left multiplication by $\rho$.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct; block decomposition of the operator along the summand and the stable-subspace lemma.

1.1 **Restriction of hard Lefschetz (a).** The inclusion $i:B_{xs}^R\to M$ and the projection $\pi:M\to B_{xs}^R$ of the summand are degree-zero bimodule maps, and they commute with left multiplication by $\rho$, since left multiplication by a central element is a bimodule endomorphism; after right reduction they remain a split inclusion and projection of the finite-dimensional real spaces. Hence the operator $L_0^i$ on $\overline M$ is block diagonal with respect to the decomposition of $\overline M$ into the summand and its complement, and each block is the corresponding power of the restricted operator. If $L_0^i$ is an isomorphism, then its inverse commutes with the block decomposition, so each diagonal block is invertible; in particular the block $\overline{B_{xs}^R}^{-i}\to\overline{B_{xs}^R}^{i}$ is an isomorphism. This holds for every $i\ge0$, which is $\mathrm{hL}(xs)$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 **The converse under the character hypotheses (b).** Assume $\mathrm{S}(<xs)$ and $\mathrm{hL}(y)$ for all $y<xs$. By [F1] the decomposition $M=B_{xs}^R\oplus\bigoplus_{y<xs}B_y^{R,a_y}$ has no shifts, and for $i<xs$ we have $\mathrm{S}(y)$; the module $B_{xs}^R$ is self-dual with symmetric Betti numbers, and by the comparison lemma the same holds for every lower summand. If $\mathrm{hL}(xs)$ holds, the block of $L_0^i$ on $B_{xs}^R$ is invertible; by hypothesis each lower block $B_y^R$ is invertible (hL$(y)$), and no other summands occur; therefore every diagonal block is invertible, so $L_0^i$ is invertible, which is $\mathrm{hL}(x,s)_0$. This proves the equivalence. [step 1.1, F1]

3.1 **Restriction of HR (c).** Assume $\mathrm{HRbar}(x,s)_0$, that is, HR for the restriction of the intersection form over a fixed reduced-word embedding of $\underline x$ and a fixed induced form of $M$; the summand $B_{xs}^R$ has symmetric Betti numbers by self-duality, and the inclusion is $L_0$-stable. Applying the stable-subspace lemma [F2] to $V=\overline{B_{xs}^R}$ inside $\overline M$ gives that the restricted operator and form satisfy hL and HR with the ambient signs; since the lowest degree of $B_{xs}^R$ equals the lowest degree $-\ell(xs)$ of $M$, the ambient standard sign is the standard sign of $B_{xs}^R$. Once $\mathrm{S}(xs)$ is known, [F3] identifies the restricted form with a positive multiple of the normalized intrinsic form, and $\mathrm{HR}(xs)$ and $\mathrm{HRbar}(xs)$ follow with no change of signs. [step 2.1, F2, F3]

4.1 **General stable subspaces (d).** The two assertions about $L_0$-stable subspaces with symmetric Betti numbers and $L_0$-stable direct summands are exactly the stable-subspace lemma [F2]; they apply to any $L_0$-stable subspace and do not use that $V$ is a tensor summand. A positive deformation $L_\zeta$ with $\zeta>0$ preserves a summand only when the summand's projector commutes with the middle-position operator, which is not automatic; when it does not, the restriction of $L_\zeta$ to the summand is not defined as an operator on the reduced summand, so no positive-parameter restriction statement is made. In particular no step identifies the restriction of $L_\zeta$ with left multiplication by $\rho$. This proves (d) and completes the lemma. [step 3.1, F2] ∎

items.title: Non-degeneracy of the local intersection forms detects Soergel's conjecture one step higher
items.statement:
Fix $x,s$ with $xs>x$ and assume $\mathrm{S}(y)$ for every $y<xs$. Put $M=B_x^RB_s^R$ and write the Kazhdan-Lusztig multiplication formula $\underline H_x\underline H_s=\underline H_{xs}+\sum_{y<xs}\mu_y\underline H_y$ with integer constants $\mu_y$. For each $y<xs$ let $E_y=\operatorname{Hom}^0(B_y^R,M)$ carry the local intersection form of [[def-local-intersection-form-for-a-soergel-summand]]. Then:

(1) $\dim_{\mathbb R}E_y=\mu_y$, while the full graded Hom module has graded rank $\langle\underline H_y,\underline H_x\underline H_s\rangle$, generally not $\mu_y$;

(2) the following are equivalent: $\mathrm{S}(xs)$; non-degeneracy of every local intersection form on $E_y$, $y<xs$; perfection of every degree-zero composition pairing $E_y\times\operatorname{Hom}^0(M,B_y^R)\to\operatorname{End}^0(B_y^R)=\mathbb R$; and equality of the actual multiplicity $a_y$ of $B_y^R$ in $M$ with $\mu_y$ for every $y<xs$.

The unconditional top summand is $B_{xs}$ with multiplicity one, and under $\mathrm{S}(<xs)$ all remaining summands are unshifted $B_y^R$. No positivity of Kazhdan-Lusztig polynomials or conjecture at $xs$ is assumed.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct; constant-term Hom formula, character comparison and the multiplicity pairing.

1.1 **The dimension of $E_y$.** By [F1] and [F2] the graded rank of $\operatorname{Hom}(B_y^R,M)$ equals $\langle h_\Delta(B_y^R),h_\nabla(M)\rangle=\langle\underline H_y,\underline H_x\underline H_s\rangle$. Expanding $\underline H_x\underline H_s=\underline H_{xs}+\sum_{z<xs}\mu_z\underline H_z$ in the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis and using the trace values of [F2], this rank equals $\sum_z\mu_z(\underline H_y,\underline H_z)$ up to the top term, whose contribution is $\delta_{y,xs}=0$ because $y<xs$; each $(\underline H_y,\underline H_z)$ lies in $v\mathbb Z[v]$ for $z\ne y$ and in $1+v\mathbb Z[v]$ for $z=y$. Hence the constant term of the graded rank is $\mu_y$, and since the graded rank lies in $\mathbb Z[v]$ with nonnegative $v$-powers, the degree-zero dimension is exactly the constant term: $\dim_{\mathbb R}E_y=\mu_y$. This is the first assertion of (1); the full graded rank is the polynomial displayed and has higher-degree terms in general, so it is not in general equal to the integer $\mu_y$. [given, F1, F2]

2.1 **The top summand and the composition pairing.** By [F1], $M=B_{xs}\oplus\bigoplus_{y<xs}B_y^{R,a_y}$ with the top summand of multiplicity one. For $y<xs$, consider a composite $B_y^R\to M\to B_y^R$ factoring through a summand other than a copy of $B_y^R$; it cannot be a nonzero scalar multiple of the identity, because rescaling such a composite would exhibit a retraction splitting $B_y^R$ off that other summand, contradicting the uniqueness of the indecomposable label. Hence only the $a_y$ copies of $B_y^R$ contribute to the scalar-coordinate pairing, and the pairing matrix is the standard evaluation pairing of rank $a_y$; by the adjoint identification of [F3] the local intersection form has the same rank. [step 1.1, F1, F3]

3.1 **Non-degeneracy and the multiplicity equalities.** By step 2.1 the local form on $E_y$ is non-degenerate if and only if its rank equals $\dim E_y$, i.e. $a_y=\mu_y$; by [F4] this is equivalent to non-degeneracy in the sense of trivial radical. Therefore non-degeneracy of every local form for all $y<xs$ is equivalent to the system of equalities $a_y=\mu_y$ for all $y<xs$, and the same rank comparison identifies this with perfection of the composition pairings. [step 2.1, F3, F4]

4.1 **The character equivalence and conclusion.** By additivity of the character and $\operatorname{ch}(B_z)=\underline H_z$ for $z<xs$, the character of $B_{xs}$ is $\operatorname{ch}(M)-\sum_{y<xs}a_y\underline H_y=\underline H_{xs}+\sum_{y<xs}(\mu_y-a_y)\underline H_y$. Since the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis is a basis of the Hecke algebra, $\operatorname{ch}(B_{xs})=\underline H_{xs}$, i.e. $\mathrm{S}(xs)$, holds if and only if $\mu_y=a_y$ for every $y<xs$. Combining with step 3.1 gives the equivalence of all four conditions in (2). [step 1.1, step 3.1, F1] ∎

items.title: Hodge-Riemann relations hold for large positive deformation, and the deformation principle
items.statement:
Let $B$ be a Soergel bimodule satisfying hL and HR with the standard sign. Then for $\zeta\gg0$ the induced operator $L_\zeta$ on $BB_s$ satisfies hL and HR with the standard sign (Theorem 5.1).

The proof contains the following **signature comparison** (Lemma 5.2): if $V,W$ are finite-dimensional graded spaces with graded non-degenerate forms and Lefschetz operators satisfying hL, $W$ is even or odd, $\dim V=(v+v^{-1})\dim W$, and $W$ satisfies HR with the standard sign, then $V$ satisfies HR with the standard sign if and only if for all $i\ge0$ the signature of the Lefschetz form on the primitive subspace $P_W^{-i+1}$ equals the signature of the Lefschetz form on all of $V^{-i}$.

Consequently (Corollary 5.3): if $\mathrm{HR}(x)$ holds and $\mathrm{hL}(x,s)_\zeta$ holds for every $\zeta\ge0$, then $\mathrm{HR}(x,s)_\zeta$ holds for every $\zeta\ge0$; more generally, if $\mathrm{hL}(x,s)_\zeta$ holds for all $\zeta\ge0$ and $\mathrm{HR}(x,s)_\zeta$ holds for a single $\zeta_0\ge0$, then $\mathrm{HR}(x,s)_\zeta$ holds for all $\zeta\ge0$. In the signature comparison use the convention $P_W^1=0$; no positive-degree primitive space is introduced.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct; a hyperbolic-block calculation and telescoping primitive signatures.

1.1 **The basis and cross blocks.** Assume $W\ne0$; the zero case has zero tensor product and is vacuous. For $i\ge0$, choose lifts $e_a\in B^{-i-1}$ of a basis of $W^{-i-1}$ orthogonal for its Lefschetz form, and lifts $p_b\in B^{-i+1}$ of a basis of $P_W^{-i+1}$; for $i=0$ the latter space is zero. Primitive decomposition (and $A:W^{-1}\to W^1$ when $i=0$) gives a basis $Ae_a,p_b$ of $W^{-i+1}$. These lifts can be included in a homogeneous right basis of $B$, so $\alpha(Ae_a),\beta(e_a),\alpha(p_b)$ reduce to a basis of $V^{-i}$, where $V=\overline{BB_s}$. By [F1]–[F2], $L_\zeta\beta(y)=\beta(Ay)$ after reduction, the $\beta$–$\beta$ Lefschetz block is zero, and $\langle\alpha(x),L_\zeta^i\beta(y)\rangle=\langle x,A^iy\rangle_W$. Consequently the $\alpha(Ae)$–$\beta(e)$ block is the invertible diagonal matrix $J=(\langle e_a,A^{i+1}e_b\rangle_W)$, while the $\alpha(p)$–$\beta(e)$ block is zero, since $A^ip=0$ for primitives in degree $-i+1$. [given, F1, F2, F3]

1.2 **The signature comparison.** For nonzero $W$, let its lowest degree be $-d$ and put $b_i=\dim W^{-i}$ for integer $i$, so $b_{-i}=b_i$. For any $V$ as in the comparison statement put $v_i=\dim V^{-i}=b_{i-1}+b_{i+1}$. Under hL, its primitive dimensions are $p_i^V=v_i-v_{i+2}=b_{i-1}-b_{i+3}$, and $p_i^W=b_i-b_{i+2}$ for $i\ge0$. The standard-HR signature required on $V^{-i}$ is the finite sum $\sum_{k\ge0}(-1)^{(d+1-i-2k)/2}p_{i+2k}^V$, in the occurring parity. Substitution and cancellation give $(-1)^{(d+1-i)/2}(b_{i-1}-b_{i+1})$ for $i\ge1$, exactly the signature of the primitive form on $P_W^{-i+1}$. For $i=0$ it is zero, since $b_{-1}=b_1$, matching $P_W^1=0$. By [F3] these signatures, together with hL, are equivalent to standard HR on $V$, proving both directions of the comparison. If $W=0$, the dimension identity forces $V=0$ and both sides are vacuous. [F3, algebra]

2.1 **The hyperbolic blocks.** The Lefschetz matrix on $V^{-i}$ therefore has form $\begin{pmatrix}C&J&E\\J&0&0\\E^{\mathsf T}&0&Q_\zeta\end{pmatrix}$. Subtracting suitable vectors from the $\beta$ block from the $\alpha(p)$ block kills $E$ without changing $Q_\zeta$; replacing the first block by itself minus one half of the corresponding $J^{-1}C$ combination of the second kills $C$. This gives a congruence to $\begin{pmatrix}0&J&0\\J&0&0\\0&0&Q_\zeta\end{pmatrix}$. The first two blocks are non-degenerate with equal positive and negative inertia. Thus the full matrix is non-degenerate exactly when $Q_\zeta$ is, and its signature is that of $Q_\zeta$. For $i=0$, $Q_\zeta$ is empty, so the matrix is already non-degenerate of signature zero for every parameter. [step 1.1, F3, algebra]

3.1 **The primitive block for $i>0$.** For the chosen lifts $p,q$ of degree $-i+1$, binomial expansion and [F1] give $\langle\alpha(p),L_\zeta^i\alpha(q)\rangle=\sum_{j=0}^i\binom{i}{j}\zeta^j\partial_s(\langle p,A^{i-j}q\rangle_B\rho^j)$ before reduction. The polynomial $\langle p,A^{i-j}q\rangle_B$ has degree $2-2j$: it vanishes for $j\ge2$, and for $j=1$ it is constant. Since $\partial_s\rho=\rho(\alpha_s^\vee)>0$, reduction yields $Q_\zeta=Q_0+\zeta i\rho(\alpha_s^\vee)Q$, where $Q$ is the definite primitive Lefschetz matrix on $P_W^{-i+1}$. If this space is zero the block is empty. Otherwise $i>0$ and $\zeta^{-1}Q_\zeta$ tends to the definite matrix $i\rho(\alpha_s^\vee)Q$; symmetric elimination near that matrix preserves the pivot signs by [F3]. Hence for sufficiently large $\zeta$, $Q_\zeta$ is definite with the signature of $Q$. There are only finitely many nonzero graded pieces, so one bound on $\zeta$ works for all of them. [step 2.1, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

4.1 **Large parameters.** Steps 2.1–3.1 make every Lefschetz form on $V^{-i}$ non-degenerate for all sufficiently large parameters, so [F3] gives hL. Their signatures are precisely the primitive signatures of $W$; step 1.2 gives HR with the standard sign on $V$. This proves the large-parameter assertion, including the empty primitive blocks and $i=0$. [step 2.1, step 3.1, step 1.2, F3]

5.1 **Deformation principle.** On any compact interval joining $\zeta_0$ to another nonnegative parameter, the polynomial family $L_\zeta$ is continuous. If hL holds throughout, [F3] transfers HR from $\zeta_0$ to that parameter. When HR$(x)$ holds, step 4.1 supplies a large positive $\zeta_0$; otherwise the more general corollary assumes one such parameter. This proves both corollaries and completes the argument without choice. [step 4.1, F3] ∎

items.title: Embedding theorem: local intersection forms are isometric to primitive Lefschetz forms
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct; the exact sequence of the top support layer, degreewise Hilbert-series comparison and adjointness. Evaluating a bimodule map at a reduced vector means evaluating its induced map on right reductions; the primitive spaces and real-valued Lefschetz forms below all belong to those reductions.

1.1 **The exact sequence and the degree-zero isomorphism.** The top support layer gives a short exact sequence $0\to\Delta_y\to B_y^R\to Q\to0$ of $\Delta$-filtered modules, and $\operatorname{Hom}(-,M)$ is left exact, so $0\to\operatorname{Hom}(Q,M)\to\operatorname{Hom}(B_y^R,M)\to\operatorname{Hom}(\Delta_y,M)$ is exact. By [F1] the three graded Hom spaces are free over $S$ and their graded ranks are additive in the $\Delta$-characters: $\operatorname{rk}\operatorname{Hom}(B_y^R,M)=\operatorname{rk}\operatorname{Hom}(Q,M)+\operatorname{rk}\operatorname{Hom}(\Delta_y,M)$ as polynomials. By [F2] all $v$-powers of $\operatorname{rk}\operatorname{Hom}(Q,M)$ are positive, so the degree-$\le0$ part of the map $\operatorname{Hom}(B_y^R,M)\to\operatorname{Hom}(\Delta_y,M)$ is injective; comparing Hilbert series degree by degree, the two free modules have equal dimension in each degree $\le0$ after restriction, and the injective degreewise map is therefore an isomorphism $\operatorname{Hom}^{\le0}(B_y^R,M)\to\operatorname{Hom}^{\le0}(\Delta_y,M)$. In particular restriction of degree-zero Hom is an isomorphism, and no full graded isomorphism is asserted. [given, F1, F2]

2.1 **Evaluation at the top and then at the bottom.** Let $c\in B_y$ be the image of the homogeneous generator of $\Delta_y\subseteq B_y$. Its reduction spans $\overline{B_y}^{\ell(y)}$: the top-layer right splitting and image equality of [F3] make its reduction nonzero. By step 1.1 restriction is an isomorphism in degree zero, so evaluation at $c$ identifies the Hom space with $(\Gamma_yM)^{\ell(y)}$, which injects into $\overline M^{\ell(y)}$ by [F3]. Thus $f\mapsto\overline{f(c)}$ is injective. Hard Lefschetz on $B_y$, part of $HR(y)$, says that $\rho^{\ell(y)}c_{\mathrm{bot}}$ is a nonzero scalar multiple of $\overline c$ in that one-dimensional top degree. Therefore $\rho^{\ell(y)}f(c_{\mathrm{bot}})$ is the same nonzero scalar multiple of $\overline{f(c)}$. If bottom evaluation vanished then top evaluation would vanish, forcing $f=0$. Finally the degree bound $\overline{B_y}^{\ell(y)+2}=0$ gives $\rho^{\ell(y)+1}c_{\mathrm{bot}}=0$; bimodule linearity makes the image primitive. This proves (1), without asserting that the multiplicity space $(\Gamma_yM)^{\ell(y)}$ is one dimensional. [step 1.1, F1, F3, F4]

3.1 **The isometry.** For $f,g\in\operatorname{Hom}^0(B_y^R,M)$, the local form is $(f,g)^{x,s}_y=g^*\circ f$, a scalar endomorphism of $B_y^R$; by the normalization of [F4], $N(f,g)^{x,s}_y=\langle g^*(f(c_{\mathrm{bot}})),\rho^{\ell(y)}c_{\mathrm{bot}}\rangle_{B_y}$, and adjointness of $g^*$ gives $\langle f(c_{\mathrm{bot}}),\rho^{\ell(y)}g(c_{\mathrm{bot}})\rangle_M=(\mathrm{ev}(f),\mathrm{ev}(g))^{-\ell(y)}_\rho$, by definition of the Lefschetz form. The factor $N$ is positive by [F4]. This proves (2). [step 2.1, F4]

4.1 **From HR to the character (3).** Assume HR$(x,s)$. Since the operator $L_0$ on $\overline M$ has $P^{-\ell(y)}_\rho$ as a primitive subspace and HR makes the Lefschetz form on it definite, the restriction of this form to the image $\mathrm{ev}(E_y)$ is non-degenerate; by the isometry of step 3.1 with the positive factor $N$, the local intersection form on $E_y$ is non-degenerate. This holds for every $y<xs$, so the detection theorem [F5], whose hypothesis $\mathrm{S}(<xs)$ is available, gives $\mathrm{S}(xs)$. This proves (3) and completes the lemma. [step 3.1, F5] ∎

items.title: Minimal positive Rouquier complexes carry the induced Hodge-Riemann signs
items.statement: Assume $\mathrm S(\le x)$ and $\mathrm{HR}(y,s)$ for every $y<x$ and simple $s$ with $ys>y$. Fix a reduced expression $\underline x$ of $x$. Then $F_x$ satisfies the Hodge-Riemann bilinear relations in the following sense: there exists an embedding as a direct summand $F_x\subseteq^{\oplus}F_{s_1}\cdots F_{s_m}$ such that for every tuple $\lambda=(\lambda_{x'})_{x'\in\pi(x,j)}$ of strictly positive real numbers and every $j\ge0$, the space $^jF_x(-j)$ embedded in $\bigoplus_{x'\in\pi(x,j)}\mathrm{BS}(x')$ carries the Hodge-Riemann bilinear relations with respect to the rescaled form $\langle-,-\rangle_\lambda$ and the Lefschetz operator given by left multiplication by $\rho$, with the global sign fixed so that the Lefschetz form is positive definite on the primitive subspaces in degrees congruent to $-m+j\pmod4$. Here $\pi(x,j)$ is the set of subexpressions of $\underline x$ obtained by deleting $j$ letters and $^jF_x(-j)\subseteq^{\oplus}\bigoplus_{x'\in\pi(x,j)}\mathrm{BS}(x')$ is the canonical summand inclusion of [F1]. The existence of such an embedding and all its sign conclusions hold for every reduced expression; no scalar comparison of the entire multiplicity-space forms from different expressions is required.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** induction over the Bruhat order; the last letter splits the complex as a summand of $F_yF_s$, the two pieces of the decomposition (6.4) are compared with the induction hypothesis and the tensoring lemma, and the source inherits the relations as a stable summand.

1.1 **Base of the induction.** [base] For $x=e$ the complex is $F_e=S$, $m=0$, and for $j=0$ the space $^0F_e(0)=S$ satisfies hL and HR trivially: its lowest degree is $0$, the primitive subspace $P^0=\mathbb R$ carries the positive definite form $\langle1,1\rangle>0$, and $0\equiv-m+j\pmod4$, so the global sign is the standard one; there are no $j\ge1$ terms. [given, F1, F4]

2.1 **Induction hypothesis and the last letter.** [ih] Fix $x\ne e$ and assume the statement for every $y<x$. Write $\underline x=s_1\cdots s_m$, $y=s_1\cdots s_{m-1}$ and $s=s_m$, so that $x=ys$ with $\ell(x)=\ell(y)+1$ and $F_x$ is a summand of $F_yF_s$; fix an embedding $F_y\subseteq^{\oplus}F_{s_1}\cdots F_{s_{m-1}}$ witnessing the induction hypothesis and use it to embed $F_x\subseteq^{\oplus}F_yF_s\subset F_{s_1}\cdots F_{s_m}$. For every $j$ this gives the embedding chain of [F1], $^jF_x(-j)\subseteq^{\oplus}{}^jF_yB_s(-j)\oplus{}^{j-1}F_y(-j+1)$, and the induction hypothesis applies to ${}^jF_y(-j)$ and to ${}^{j-1}F_y(-j+1)$ with the global signs indexed by $y$; by [F2] the $j$-th term of $F_x$ is linear. [given, step 1.1, F1, F2]

3.1 **The decomposition of the middle term and orthogonality.** Under $\mathrm S(\le x)$ the comparison lemma gives a decomposition of the multiplicity space, so ${}^jF_y(-j)=\bigoplus_{z}V_z\otimes_\mathbb RB_z$ with degree-zero multiplicity spaces $V_z$; define $B^\uparrow=\bigoplus_{zs>z}V_z\otimes B_z$ and $B^\downarrow=\bigoplus_{zs<z}V_z\otimes B_z$, so that ${}^jF_y(-j)=B^\uparrow\oplus B^\downarrow$. The decomposition is orthogonal for the induced form because $\operatorname{Hom}(B^\uparrow,D B^\downarrow)=\operatorname{Hom}(B^\downarrow,DB^\uparrow)=0$ for non-isomorphic indecomposables under $\mathrm S$; character calculations give that $B^\uparrow B_s$ is perverse and that $B^\downarrow B_s\cong B^\downarrow(-1)\oplus B^\downarrow(1)$. [step 2.1, F2, F3]

4.1 **The shifted descent piece does not contribute.** In the decomposition $B^\downarrow B_s\cong B^\downarrow(1)\oplus B^\downarrow(-1)$ the restriction of the Lefschetz form to $B^\downarrow(1)$ is identically zero: left multiplication by $\rho$ satisfies hL on $B^\downarrow$ (the induction hypothesis gives hL on ${}^jF_y(-j)$, and its unshifted block projectors commute with $\rho$, so each descent block inherits hL), so [F5] applies to the shifted piece with $d>0$. Moreover the projection of ${}^jF_x(-j)$ to $B^\downarrow B_s$ lands entirely in $B^\downarrow(1)$: ${}^jF_x(-j)$ lives in perverse degree $0$ by the linearity theorem, and Hom-vanishing between perverse degrees $0$ and $-1$ forces the projection to the $B^\downarrow(-1)$-part to vanish. Hence the image of ${}^jF_x(-j)$ in $B^\downarrow B_s$ contributes nothing to the Lefschetz form. [step 3.1, F2, F5]

5.1 **All Lefschetz forms and a genuine split inclusion.** The projection onto the surviving factors defines a degree-zero $\rho$-equivariant map $\jmath:{}^jF_x(-j)\to B^\uparrow B_s\oplus{}^{j-1}F_y(-j+1)$. For every $k\ge0$ and $b,b'$ in source degree $-k$, step 4.1 gives
$\langle b,\rho^kb'\rangle=\langle\jmath(b),\rho^k\jmath(b')\rangle$,
since the omitted shifted-descent factor contributes zero to that Lefschetz form. This is equality of all negative-degree Lefschetz forms, not a degree-one form identity. Applying $q$ to the original split inclusion yields a split inclusion; every map from its perverse source to $B^\downarrow(1)$ vanishes after $q$, since none of those differently shifted indecomposable classes are isomorphic. Hence $q(\jmath)$ is split injective. Lift a left inverse to a morphism $h$ of bimodules. Then $q(h\jmath)=1$, so reflection of isomorphisms by the radical quotient makes $h\jmath$ invertible. The map $(h\jmath)^{-1}h$ is a genuine bimodule left inverse of $\jmath$. Thus $\jmath$ is a split inclusion already before reduction and remains injective after reduction. [step 4.1, F2]

6.1 **The codomain satisfies the relations with the global sign.** The two orthogonal summands of the codomain are handled as follows. The summand ${}^{j-1}F_y(-j+1)$ satisfies HR with the global sign of the induction hypothesis for $y$ and $j-1$, namely positivity on primitive degrees congruent to $-\ell(y)+(j-1)=-m+1+j-1=-m+j\pmod4$, which is the required global sign for $x,j$. The summand $B^\uparrow B_s$ satisfies HR by the tensoring lemma [F3]: $B^\uparrow$ is a self-dual direct sum of normalized $B_z$ with $zs>z$, each satisfying $\mathrm{HR}(z,s)$ by hypothesis and hence hL and HR with the standard sign; its restricted form satisfies HR with the inherited global sign by the induction hypothesis and the stable-subspace lemma. Multiply this form by its global factor $\varepsilon\in\{\pm1\}$ to give the standard sign, apply [F3], and undo that same factor on the induced tensor form. The tensor thus has the inherited global sign shifted by one, i.e. positivity on degrees congruent to $(-\ell(y)+j)-1=-m+j\pmod4$. Since the two summands are orthogonal and carry the same global sign, the codomain satisfies HR with the global sign fixed by $-m+j$. [step 5.1, step 2.1, F3]

7.1 **Inheritance from the negative-degree form identities.** The reduced map $\jmath$ is an injective $\rho$-equivariant graded map into the HR space of step 6.1. Its source has symmetric dimensions by [F2] and normalized self-duality, so ambient hL makes every $\rho^k$ on source degree $-k$ injective, hence an isomorphism onto the opposite degree. Source primitives map into ambient primitives. The identity for every $k$ in step 5.1 therefore makes each source primitive form definite with the required ambient sign. Primitive decomposition on the source now gives nonsingular Lefschetz forms in every negative degree; together with hL and graded symmetry this also proves that its original restricted invariant form is non-degenerate. Thus it satisfies HR. The embedding was chosen before the positive rescalings: the induction gives the properties for every tuple on $F_y$, the orthogonal label blocks are independent of these scalars, and the split projection argument is categorical. Applying this argument for every tuple proves the full simultaneous rescaling assertion and closes the induction. [step 5.1, step 6.1, F2, F4, discharge-induction: step 2.1] ∎

items.title: The minimal Rouquier differential supplies the injectivity input of the weak-Lefschetz substitute
items.statement:
(1) **Right-module retraction.** For every $x$ and every reduced expression of $x$, the minimal Rouquier complex $F_x$ is homotopy equivalent, as a complex of graded right $S$-modules, to the single right module $S(-\ell(x))$ concentrated in cohomological degree $0$. Consequently the right reduction has $H^0(\overline{F_x})\cong\mathbb R(-\ell(x))$, one copy of $\mathbb R$ in internal degree $\ell(x)$, and $H^j(\overline{F_x})=0$ for $j\ne0$.

(2) **Injectivity criterion.** Let $C$ be a bounded below complex of graded free right $S$-modules with $C^{-1}=0$ whose right reduction satisfies $H^{-1}(\overline C)=0$ and whose $H^0(\overline C)$ is concentrated in a single internal degree $d$. Then the reduced first differential $\overline{d^0}:\overline{C^0}\to\overline{C^1}$ is injective in every internal degree $\ne d$; in particular it is injective in internal degrees $\le d-1$. The conclusion is unchanged if $C$ is replaced by a homotopy-equivalent complex $C'$ with $C'^{-1}=0$ obtained by cancelling contractible two-term summands whose source lies in a positive cohomological degree, in particular the contractible shifted-descent summands occurring in the zero-parameter hard-Lefschetz theorem.

(3) **Application to the ascent differential.** Let $xs>x$ and assume $\mathrm S(\le x)$. Then the first differential of the complex $F_xF_s$, whose source is $B_x^RB_s^R$ and whose target is $^1F_xB_s\oplus B_x^R(1)$, has reduced form injective in internal degrees $\le\ell(x)$. The complex $F_xF_s$ need not itself be minimal, and no minimality is used in the conclusion.

(4) **Separation of inputs.** The form compatibility $\langle b,L_\zeta b'\rangle=\langle\varphi b,\varphi b'\rangle_\gamma$ and the operator commutation $\varphi(L_\zeta b)=L\varphi(b)$ used in the hard-Lefschetz proof are independent additional inputs that must be verified separately using the deleted-word factorization and the induced forms; in the zero-parameter descent case the form on the shifted descent piece vanishes and the hard-Lefschetz argument must separate the kernel of $d_3$ rather than apply the criterion of (2) to the whole target.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct; the split rank-one retraction, its tensor product over a reduced word, and the kernel-of-the-first-differential computation on reduced right-module complexes.

1.1 **The rank-one retraction.** In the right basis $(c_{\mathrm{id}},c_s)$ of $B_s^R$ we have $\varepsilon_s(c_{\mathrm{id}}a+c_sb)=a+b\alpha_s$ for $a,b\in S$. The section $\sigma(r)=c_{\mathrm{id}}\cdot r$ satisfies $\varepsilon_s\sigma(r)=r$, so $\varepsilon_s$ is split surjective and $B_s^R=\sigma(S(1))\oplus\ker(\varepsilon_s)$ as right $S$-modules; the subcomplex $\sigma(S(1))\xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }S(1)$ of $F_s$ is contractible, and $\ker(\varepsilon_s)$ is a direct summand of the complex $F_s$ concentrated in degree $0$. The kernel is $\{c_{\mathrm{id}}(-\alpha_sb)+c_sb\}=\{(c_s-c_{\mathrm{id}}\alpha_s)b\}$, so it is free of rank one as a right $S$-module with generator $c_s-c_{\mathrm{id}}\alpha_s=(\alpha_s\otimes1-1\otimes\alpha_s)/2$ of internal degree $1$; hence $\ker(\varepsilon_s)\cong S(-1)$ as a graded right $S$-module and $F_s\simeq S(-1)$ in the homotopy category of complexes of graded right $S$-modules. [given, F1, F3]

1.2 **The injectivity criterion.** Let $C$ be as in (2) and let $c\in\overline{C^0}$ be homogeneous of internal degree $D$ with $\overline{d^0}(c)=0$. Then $c$ is a cocycle, so it represents a class $[c]\in H^0(\overline C)$; since $H^{-1}(\overline C)=0$ and $C^{-1}=0$, the zeroth cohomology is the cokernel of no incoming map and $[c]$ vanishes if and only if $c$ lies in the image of $\overline{d^{-1}}$, which is zero because $C^{-1}=0$. Hence $[c]\ne0$ forces $D$ to be the single internal degree $d$ in which $H^0(\overline C)$ is concentrated; therefore a nonzero kernel element can occur only in degree $d$, and the map is injective in every other degree, in particular in degrees $\le d-1$. If $C'$ is homotopy equivalent to $C$ with $C'^{-1}=0$ and is obtained by cancelling contractible two-term summands whose source lies in positive cohomological degree, then $C'^0=C^0$ for the cancellation in degrees $\ge1$, the reductions $\overline{C'}$ and $\overline C$ are homotopy equivalent by [F3], so $H^{-1}(\overline{C'})=0$ and $H^0(\overline{C'})$ is concentrated in degree $d$, and the same argument applies to $C'$. This proves (2). [given, F3]

2.1 **The retraction for a reduced word.** Write $\underline x=s_1\cdots s_m$. For $m=0$ the complex is $S$. For $m>0$, tensor the right-$S$-linear homotopy equivalence $F_{s_1}\simeq S(-1)$ of step 1.1 with the remaining bimodule complex $G=F_{s_2}\cdots F_{s_m}$. This is legitimate because the maps and homotopies on the first factor are right linear; signed totalization preserves the homotopy identities. As a complex of right modules, $S(-1)\otimes_S G\cong G(-1)$. Repeating on the first remaining factor gives $F_{s_1}\cdots F_{s_m}\simeq S(-m)$. No left action is assigned to a right-module retraction and no right-linear map is tensored as a map on the second factor. Forgetting the left action of the bimodule homotopy equivalence from $F_x$ to this word complex proves (1). Applying the additive reduction functor preserves these homotopy identities, so the reduced cohomology is a single copy of $\mathbb R$ in internal degree $m$. [step 1.1, F2, F3]

3.1 **Application to $F_xF_s$.** Let $xs>x$ and assume $\mathrm S(\le x)$. By [F2] the concatenated word is reduced for $xs$, so $F_xF_s\cong F_{xs}$ in $K^b$, and by step 2.1 applied to $xs$ the complex $F_{xs}$ is homotopy equivalent over right $S$-modules to $S(-\ell(xs))=S(-\ell(x)-1)$ concentrated in cohomological degree $0$. Hence $C:=F_xF_s$ satisfies the hypotheses of (2) with $d=\ell(x)+1$: it is bounded below, $C^{-1}=0$, and its reduction has $H^{-1}=0$ with $H^0$ one copy of $\mathbb R$ in internal degree $\ell(x)+1$. By step 1.2 the reduced first differential $\overline{d^0}$ is injective in internal degrees $\le\ell(x)$, which is (3); note that $F_xF_s$ has the terms $C^0=B_x^RB_s^R$ and $C^1={}^1F_xB_s\oplus B_x^R(1)$ by [F2], and that no minimality of $F_xF_s$ was used, only the homotopy equivalence with $F_{xs}$. [step 2.1, step 1.2, F2]

4.1 **Stability under cancellation and the descent caveat.** If the zero-parameter hard-Lefschetz proof cancels a contractible summand of $F_xF_s$ whose source lies in cohomological degree $\ge1$ (the shifted descent piece), the surviving complex $C'$ has $C'^{-1}=0$, is homotopy equivalent to $C$ and has $\overline{C'}$ homotopy equivalent to $\overline C$, so step 1.2 applies and the reduced first differential of $C'$ is still injective in internal degrees $\le\ell(x)$; this is the "splitting off contractible summands with zero degree-zero source" clause of (2). On the other hand the form identity $\langle b,L_\zeta b'\rangle=\langle\varphi(b),\varphi(b')\rangle_\gamma$ and the commutation $\varphi(L_\zeta b)=L\varphi(b)$ do not follow from the right-module retraction: they are identities between maps of bimodules involving the induced forms and the deleted-word factorization, and they must be verified in the hard-Lefschetz theorem using [F4]; for $\zeta=0$ on a descent summand the Lefschetz form of the shifted piece is identically zero, so the theorem restricts the weak-Lefschetz substitute to the kernel of $d_3$ instead of the whole target. This completes the proof of (3) and (4). [step 3.1, F4] ∎
